speechtext:

2.	(a) It having been reported to the department that successful methods in the retraining of disabled soldiers had been adopted in England the introduction of which was being advocated in Canada, W. E. Segsworth, previously Director of Vocational Training and T. A. Stevenson, Assistant Director Information and Service Branch (who also represents the Trades and Labour Council of Canada with regard to the industrial retraining of ex-members of the Forces) were sent to England in April 1919, their instructions being to investigate the methods of industrial retraining applied in England; the relationship between organized labour and the Governmental agencies conducting such retraining, and the relationship between organized labour and ex-members of the Forces undergoing such retraining, particularly with respect to the permanent reabsorption of trainees into commercial or industrial life as civilians.
Mr. Segsworth was also appointed to proceed as the representative of the department to the Inter-Allied Conference at Rome which was convened for the purpose of discussing the problem of the rehabilitation of disabled soldiers. It was considered that advantage might be taken of methods which had proven successful in other countries. It was also the desire of those responsible for the conference that definite records of the work conducted by the department in Canada be made available to representatives of other countries confronted with similar problems.
The expenses of Messrs. Segsworth and Stevenson amounted to $3,603.36.
(b) For the purpose of negotiating arrangements whereby former members of the Imperial Forces resident in Canada (numbering about 50,000) would receive at the expense of the Imperial Government post war benefits administered by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and whereby ex-members of the Canadian Forces resident in the United Kingdom (numbering about 20,000) would receive at the expense of the Canadian Government post war benefits made available in England by the Imperial .Government, E. H. Scammell, Assistant Deputy Minister, was instructed to proceed to England in May 1919. As a result of the arrangements he made ex-mem-

bers of the Forces in both countries now obtain benefits with greater convenience than would otherwise have been the case, and considerable savings have been effected in administrative expenses.
The expenses of Mir. E. H. Scammell amounted to $1,148.51.
(c) It having been represented to the department that owing to the heavy demands on the British Government in providing artificial limbs, orthopaedic boots and other orthopaedic appliances for former members of the Imperial Forces, discharged Canadian soldiers resident in the United Kingdom were not being furnished with such appliances as rapidly as might be desired, F. G. Robinson, Deputy Minister and R. W. Coult-hard, Director of Orthopaedic and Surgical Appliances, were sent to England in January, 1920, for the purpose of investigating the desirability of operating in England a Branch Orthopaedic Fitting Depot, similar to thosie operated by the department throughout Canada for the issue of artificial limbs, orthopaedic boots and other orthopaedic appliances. They were also instructed thoroughly to investigate the methods adapted by the British and French Governments in connection with the supply and maintenance of artificial limbs and the design thereof, so that advantage might be taken in Canada of any improved methods or designs not previously applied here.
The deputy minister was also instructed to negotiate with officials of the British Government certain adjustments relative to the administration of benefits to ex-members of the Forces by the British and Canadian Governments reciprocally, the desirability of which had arisen, as the work developed out of experience in applying under constantly varying conditions the general principles previously agreed upon. Mr. Robinson was further instructed to arrange with officials of the British Government the rates at which the Canadian Government would be reimbursed by the British Government for services rendered by the depaitment on their behalf to ex-members of the Imperial Forces resident in Canada; 'and to investigate the conditions under which ex-members of the Canadian Forces, resident in the United Kingdom, who have been disabled by war service, were receiving benefits through the British Government, and to make any necessary recommendations in this respect.

Consideration of an amendment made by the Senate to Bill No. 29 respecting Honey.
Hon. NEWTON W. ROWELL (Minister of Health):	Mr. Speaker, the Senate has
added a section to this Bill, No. 4, the effect of which is to provide that the penalties under the Food and Drugs Act shall apply to the violation of the provisions of this Act in lieu of the penalties under the Criminal Code, which otherwise would be applicable. There ns no objection to the change made by the Senate; probably on the whole it is an improvement. The only point is that the Senate has not made the amendment wholly efficacious to accomplish the purpose intended. Therefore I desire to slightly modify the Senate amendment.
Mr. Speaker, might I ask the hon. President of the Privy Council to speak in a louder tone of voice? His remarks are quite inaudible at this end of the Chamber, and we do not know what- is going on.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Senate has amended the Bill by adding a new section, Number 4, the effect of which is to provide that the penalties under the Food and Drugs Act shall apply to violations of this Act in lieu of the penalties which would be applicable under the Criminal Code in the absence of this specific provision. I see no objection to the Senate amendment; it is probably, on the whole, wise that the same penalty should apply to violations of this Act as apply to violations of the Food and Drugs Act. But the form of the amendment made by the Senate is hardly such as to accomplish the purpose in view. I therefore move to vary it by striking out the words " section 2 or" in the first line thereof and inserting in the first line after the word " who," the following:
is guilty of wilful adulteration of honey under section 2. or who-

The effect of the change will he as follows. The clause as amended by the Senate reads:
Every one who violates any provision of section 2 or 3 of this Act is guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to the penalties provided by section 16 of the Food and Drugs Act, 1920.
When amended as now proposed, it will read as follows:
Every one who is guilty of wilful adulteration of honey under section 2 or who violates any provision of section 3 of this Act is guilty of an offence and liable upon summary conviction to the penalties provided by section 16 of the Food and Drugs Act, 1920.
The Department of Justice has advised that this amendment should be made.

What are the
penalties provided by section 16 of the Food and Drugs Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are as follows:
If the adulteration is deemed to be injurious to health within the meaning of the Act, for a first offence, upon summary conviction a fine not exceeding $200 and costs and not less than $50 and costs or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months, or to both fine and imprisonment; and for each subsequent offence, a fine not exceeding $500 and costs and not less than $50 and costs, or to imprisonment for a term .not exceeding six months or to both fine and imprisonment. If the adulteration is not deemed to be injurious to health, the provision is, a fine not exceeding $100 and costs and not less- than $25 and costs, or imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months; and for each subsequent offence a fine not exceeding $200 and costs and not less than $50 and costs, or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months, or to both fine and imprisonment.

Why is there no provision
for penalty in the case of adulteration of honey after it is made by the bees? There is provision here against feeding sugar to the bees, but there is nothing to prevent the beekeeper from adulterating the honey after it is produced.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few observations to make-
The speech of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) wa9 'nterrupted at this point by

the prolonged applause which greeted the entrance into the Chamber to take his seat for the first time this session of the Kt. Hon. Sir E. L. Borden, Prime Minister, who had been absent by reason of illness.

I am delighted Mr. Speaker, that the good luck has fallen to a member of the Opposition to be in position to welcome the Prime Minister back to the House. Just at that point where we had the delightful experience of welcoming the Prime Minister upon his return, I was addressing you, Sir, upon the Bill now before the House.
What I would like to say-and I direct my remarks particularly to the Minister of Justice, who has charge of this Bill-is that it is not desirable to be amending the constitution and powers of the courts unless it is absolutely necessary to do so. The Supreme Court Act is quite an old enactment. It has been amended a few times, but not very often. The Prime Minister, who is now in his seat, the Minister of Justice, and every lawyer in this House, know that it is exceedingly desirable that the practice and procedure of the courts should continue without very much change. The Supreme Court of Canada is not like a provincial court; it is a court to which all provinces look as an appellate court, and for that reason it is desirable that the practice and procedure and constitution of that court should be well known and well established.
Unless there is most urgent necessity, any change in the constitution of the court, which change would necessarily mean a change in practice, should be avoided and should be indulged in as seldom as possible. (Lawyers in this House know that text-books have been written on the Supreme Court Act and that those text-books are in the libraries of lawyers from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Those text-books endeavour to show as clearly as possible the powers and the practice of the court. Several points in regard to the jurisdiction of the court and the scope of it have been settled, upon the old Act, by decisions of the Privy (Council. For these reasons it is highly desirable that those text-books which have (been written on the old Act and decisions rendered by the Privy Council along those lines should be held as authorities and that nothing should be done by us, unless it is absolutely necessary to do so, which would have the effect of destroying the interpretations which have -been given to the Act and also of destroying the
[Mr. McKenzie.}
usefulness of the text-books I have mentioned .

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is a volume of conversation going on, not only on the floor of this Chamber, but I regret to say, in other parts of the Chamber. I would ask that more consideration be shown to the business of the House.	[DOT]

I have read the Supreme Court Act several times before, but I have read it recently and I have also read the amendments made in different years and the amendments that are now proposed. I am not quite convinced that the amendments now proposed are highly necessary. They may be, and possibly the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) will explain the necessity for them. With these remarks, which will appeal to lawyers, if not to other people, I should like the minister to bear in mind that we should interfere as little as possible with the constitution and the established practice of the court. Every hon. member who is in any particular calling knows that he does not want the tools to which he is accustomed, changed. We have had a good deal of talk about containers of food, of fish, farming' implements and all that sort of thing, and a great deal of dissatisfaction is occasioned if there is any undue interference. We are now in the field where we are tampering with the implements of the trade of the much maligned lawyer. I am only anxious that lawyers should be protected as much as is possible by our not interfering with the proper administration of justice as regards this oourt.

speakeroldname: Et. Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) :
speechtext: Mr. (Speaker-

Before the minister
speaks, I must direct the attention of the House to the fact that if the minister exercises his right to reply, the debate is closed. Therefore, if any hon. member desires to speak on this matter, he should do so now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
-I fully appreciate and share the views of the hon. gentleman as to the undesirability of unnecessarily modifying the law prescribing the duties, functions and powers of the Supreme Court. I realize also the importance of not making modifications which imay render inapplicable decisions which have been made in the past, or possibly the observations of textbooks written upon them. But I desire to point out that the purpose of this Bill is one of simplification. It does not affect the

constitution of the court; it affects the jurisdiction of the court, and its principal purpose is to make that jurisdiction the same with regard to cases coming fro'm any of the provinces. Its second purpose is to simplify the provisions that now determine that jurisdiction. As the hon. member has said, the Supreme Court Act has, from time to time, been the subject of amendment, and if one looks at it in its present condition, it is evident that some, at all events, of the amendments that have been made, have been made from the point of view of meeting particular cases that have arisen. The result is that you have these provisions for particular cases bearing upon the question of jurisdiction and dealing with that question in that way, producing, I think, a lack of clearness. This Bill is introduced at the suggestion of the judges of the court, and as a result of their experience in the application of the law. As I have said, its principal purpose is to make the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court applicable to the same classes of cases without distinction between the provinces from which those cases come, and that in itself is a desirable thing. Its second purpose is, as I have said, to simplify the form of the sections in which the jurisdiction is defined, so as to reduce the cases down to limited classes which will cover all the cases intended to be covered without the necessity of having specific provisions for particular kinds of cases.

speechtext:
I desire to move to
amend subparagraph (a) by striking out the word "and" in the last line thereof and adding the following:
Provided that except in cases in which such highest court of final resort has concurrent jurisdiction with the court from which it is sought to appeal, special leave shall not be granted in any case which is not appealable to such highest court of last resort and which has not been heretofore appealable to the Supreme Court; and,
The purpose of the amendment is to correct the provision as it stood, which would have produced a Tesult which was not intended. Under the section as it stands in the Bill, cases involving small amounts in the different provinces which are not appealable within the province would have been appealable to the Supreme Court on leave of the court of last resort in the province. There was no intention to produce, and I do not think there would be any justification for producing that result, and it is to prevent that that I am proposing this amendment.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On section 41-leave of provincial court of last resort:

His Majesty enjoys certain privileges before the courts, but I think it is giving him an unfair advantage to grant this privilege which is refused to the ordinary citizen. I have in mind cases of damages against the Crown, for instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In so far as His Majesty is given any special right here, it is a right he already has. These classes of cases mentioned here are appealable under the law as it stands, without anybody's leave. At the present time for the provinces other than Quebec $1,000 is the amount fixed for the "de piano" right of appeal. This Bill for the "de piano" right as regards all provinces makes it $2,000, but in other cases there may be an appeal by leave of the court of last resort of the provinces. The reason why a special provision is made for all the classes of cases enumerated in the present section is that there was in all these cases a right to appeal "de piano," and it was thought that to subject that absolute right as it now stands to the condition that there should be leave to appeal given by the highest court of last resort in the province might in certain cases be looked upon as depriving those parties of a very substantial right, and upon that consideration we have this provision, that even if the court of last resort in the provinces does not, with regard to that particular class of cases, think an appeal ought to be granted, it is possible for the Supreme Court to grant it. I do not know whether it is very necessary, but it is put there because in the opinion of the judges it would remove any ground for suggesting that the parties to these particular classes of cases who had this exceptional right of appeal "de piano" were being deprived of resort to the Supreme Court.

On section 3-when appeal shall be brought.

This section amends section 69 of the Supreme Court Act by adding the following words to that section:
Provided that the months of July and August shall he excluded In the computation of the said sixty days.
Will the minister be kind enough to explain this section in detail?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The delay of sixty days is prescribed for certain classes of cases where an application is necessary, and within which time it must be made. This provision is made to meet the fact that July and August are very generally looked upon in the legal profession as vacation months; and in fact, under the laws of some provinces, these months are not included in the delays prescribed for taking certain steps in procedure. I do not say that this is true in all cases. The hon. member knows there are exceptional cases, but this is the general rule, and it was considered fair to make this provision so that the months of July and August, in regard to the particular delay of sixty days referred to in this section, should not count. Difficulties have arisen and people have found their rights jeopardized, and this provision seems to me but reasonable.
Does the minister not think that this is.adding to the law's delays?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So long as the long vacation exists I am afraid it will add to the law's delays. I can say that in the opinion of the judges of the court, as well as in my opinion, this is a desirable provision to meet practical conditions that exist.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 32 carry?

I wish to make a few observations in regard, to this section, and in doing so I shall apply my remarks largely to the old settled section of the country, the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec, and more particularly Ontario.
This section is an absolute departure from the practice which has prevailed in the preparation of lists in Ontario except as that practice was varied by the Wartime Elections Act. It is a decided departure from good and safe principles. It has been recognized in this country for many years that the provincial lists which were in force sixty days before nomination day were the lists used at federal elections. There were some objections taken to these lists being used, because in some cases they were a year or more than a year old and men who were entitled to vote were not on the lists. But there is this to be said: they were prepared by non-partisan men; they were prepared by municipal authorities. Party spirit did not enter into their operation at all. These lists-and this applies also to the preparation of lists in the rural parts of Ontario-were revised by the county judge; no one could say that they were not revised in a fair and upright manner. I do not think that any clause in the Act is more important than this clause,
because no matter how broad you make your franchise-and we have made it so broad under our recent laws that it includes every man and every woman twenty-one years of age who is a British subject-no matter how fair you are in the appointment of your returning officers (and I think some improvement could have been made in the Bill in that respect) if your voters' lists are not prepared in a fair and honourable and open manner by non-partisan officials, the very springs of our representative institutions are going to be fouled.
Now, I say that under clause 32 the old principle has been absolutely departed from. In the first place, in the rural parts of Ontario, enumerators-they are called by the more euphonious name of "registrars" in this Bill-are going to be appointed by returning officers who are nominees of this Government or any Government that is in power, which nominees are certain to be partisan officers. The returning officer will be chosen because he is a partisan officer, because he will help the party in power to win the election. I do not say that he is going to do that dishonestly, but I do say that all his sympathies and all his energies will be devoted to doing anything possible within the limits of the law, even with a stretching of the law, sometimes, to see that the party to whom he owes his appointment is returned to power. Under this Bill the returning officer is given the right to name the registrars. As a matter of human nature and as a matter of course, in every riding in this country registrars are going to be appointed who have at heart the interests of the party in power, and who are going to endeavour as far as they can to help advance those interests. As a matter of fact, the registrar is going to become a paid canvasser, I contend, for the Government in power, and his expenses are going to be paid by the people of Canada. I contend that that establishes, so far as the Government are concerned, nothing more or less than practically a large fund that can be improperly used. We heard not so very long ago members on the other side of the House complain about my friends to my left having large campaign funds for the assisting of their candidates at elections. But this provision of the Bill is a far more dangerous provision as a campaign fund to assist the Government than contributions made by individual farmers, as was the case in the constituency of Assiniboia and as may take place in any constituency in which a farmer candidate is running. What does it mean, Mr. Chairman? It means that throughout the Do-

minion o! Canada there will be established under this law-I am making only a rough estimate-about thirty thousand polling subdivisions. Under the Act of 1911, when women had not the vote, there were over thirteen thousand polling subdivisions. Under this Act, with the number of voters doubled and the limit of the number of polls put at 300, I do not think that my estimate of from 25,000 to 30,000 polling subdivisions is out of the way. So we come down to this situation: that the Government starts out in the election with the appointment of 25,000 or 30,000 registrars practically as their agents for the purpose of adding names of voters to the lists. I say again that these men will be paid, under the schedule which is attached to the Act, from $50 to $60 each; they become paid canvassers for the party in power. And that is not all. Under this Act these men are given far more power; they are given a more autocratic power, than they were given under the War-time Elections Act.
For instance, under the old Act, the registrar in the Yukon made changes and added names only on statutory declarations. Under this Bill, the registrar is given power to make changes on the representations of any credible witness. Under the old Act, the War-time Elections Act, bad as it was, in Nova Scotia, if the registrar added or struck off names, there was a right to appeal. Under this Bill, there is no right to appeal whatever as regards the rural parts of a constituency; the registrar has absolute discretion whether a man's name shall be added to the list or not, or whether a man's name shall be struck fiom the list or not, and it is only known nine or ten days from polling day whether that man's name is on the list or not. There is no opportunity for a 'man whose name is not on the list to get in his vote except that under clause 63 of the Bill he may get in his vote. But the benefits given by clause 63 in that regard are not by any means as great as the disadvantage that would ensue if clause 63 is allowed to remain as it is.
My first contention is that if we are going to have public faith maintained in our representative institutions, we must start out at the very spring and see what these voters' lists are absolutely fair and that nothing remains in the public mind to make them think that the lists are prepared in a partisan way for the purpose of aiding the Government in power. The preparation of the lists should be done impartially by a judicial authority as it was done in the

past, and it should not be left to the mere discretion of a partisan officer.
My second contention is that the expense in connection with the preparation of these lists is going to be very large, and at this time of this country's history when we have to look after every thousand dollars and should look after the millions more particularly and considering the fact that this enumeration will cost in the neighbourhood of a million dollars, we Bhould not encourage any system of preparation of lists which has the disadvantage that I have already pointed out and which has the additional disadvantge of putting a large burden of expense upon this country. I took the trouble of looking into the cost of the enumeration at the last election. In that election we had some 234 constituencies, in thirty-two of which members were elected by acclamation. In the balance of those constituencies contests took place. I find by looking at the Auditor General's Report, that the cost of the enumeration at the election of 1917 was $685,555. If we calculate on that basis the cost of enumeration for the thirty-two constituencies had contests taken place in them, I figure that the cost of enumeration for the 234 constituencies would have been at least $800,000. I have a statement here prepared by the Provincial Auditor of Ontario on behalf of the treasurer of that province from which statement I find that at the last election in Ontario the total expense of enumeration in that province alone was $518,266.77, This is another good and valid reason why the old system should be adopted and we should go back to the preparation of lists by the provincial authorities. If the lists in Ontario cost $518,266.77 for enumeration alone, and you consider Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick as being together equal in population to Ontario, we shall find that the lists in those four provinces will cost at least $1,000,090 for enumeration alone at the next election. But that is not all. If I read the Bill aright and go forward to clause 101 under which lists have to be prepared under the Canada Temper aruce Act for taking a referendum, and if the lists are prepared by the system which the Acting Solicitor General suggests in this Bill, it is hard to say what expense this country will be put to, because every time a referendum takes place under the Canada Temperance Act, lists will have to be prepared under this Bill and the province which asks for the referendum will not have to pay the expense, but the expense will be borne by the Dominion Government. There-

m3
fore, on the ground of expense alone, we should seek some fairer and more economical method of preparing the lists. Affairs in Toronto at the present time are in a condition of flux; but wte have before the Ontario Legislature a very fair Bill as regards the preparation of lists. This Bill is in the name of Mr. Drury, and I have no doubt that it will be passed. As an additional argument in support of my contention that we should go back from the system of enumeration to the old system of preparation of lists by local authorities, I need only point out that the Ontario- Government, after one experience, has thrown aside the enumeration system and has reverted to the old system. The system adopted in the new Ontario legislation, which I am sure will become the law of Ontario in a few days or a couple of weeks, is simply this, and it will so correspond -with our old franchise and will work in so nicely with our Act that I plead with the Acting Solicitor General to adopt it in the preparation of our lists as a matter of fairness and economy. Under the new Ontario legislation, the municipal authorities in preparing the assessment roll, are compelled to put on that assessment roll the name of every man or wom-an of twenty-one years of age; that roll is then transcribed by the clerk of the municipality and is made into a municipal voters' list for municipal purposes. That list is then subject to revision by the -Court of Revision of the municipality, and then -it is subject to revision, as in the olden- days, as my hon. friend is well aware, by a judge of the county court. In the case of a general election or in the case of a by-election on account of the death or resignation -of a member of the Ontario Legislature, under this new provincial legislation, an election board is appointed in each county consisting of officials such as the county judge, and the deputy registrar, five in all. As soon as a dissolution occurs, or a writ is issued on account of a vacancy in the Assembly this board proceeds at once with the municipal lists which have been prepared as I have described, and it prepares the list fo-r the election of members to the legislature. Nothing could be simpler, faireir or more economical as regards this Government, because this will cost them practically nothing the work being all done and paid for by t-he municipal authorities. The only expense to be incurred would be this, that in the case of a dissolution of this Houe o-r in the case of the issue of a writ, this Government would have to pay the election board some expenses in connection with the revision of 148
the lists prepared by the municipal authorities. This is a matter which the committee should consider very carefully. The Acting Solicitor General has repeatedly, in the course of this discussion said that he wants these lists to be absolutely fair; that he does not want anything of a partisan nature to enter into this legislation; that he wanits, in effect, the people of this country to have confidence in our institutions by knowing that out lists are prepared in a capable, honest and unpartisan fashion. I do not think any amendment -can be suggested to this House that will give the public more confidence in this Administration than the suggestion I have made in regard to the preparation of the lists. Without saying more, I will give notice that at some time in the course of the discussion on this Bill, not now unless some other arrangement is made, I shall move an amendment along these lines, though perhaps noit in these very words:
That section 32 be amended by the addition; of the following subsection, called 32A:
Notwithstanding anything in this Act contained, for the purpose of any Dominion election held within the limits of the province of Ontario, the voters' lists shall, except as hereinafter provided, be those prepared and completed for municipal purposes for the several polling subdivisions under the laws of the province of Ontario, and which were at the date of the issue of the writ for said election under such laws in force for municipal purposes, and all persons named therein as entitled to vote for members of the Legislative Assembly, unless disentitled by the terms of this Act, shall he entitled to vote for members of the House of Commons, provided always that to the said lists there may he added all persons qualified to vote under this Act and there may be subtracted all persons disentitled to vote under this Act, and in revising such lists and making such additions and subtractions, the provisions of the laws of the province of Ontario regulating the revision and bringing into force of the provincial voters' lists in such case shall as far as possible he observed and followed. In such parts of the province of Ontario as are without municipal organization, the voters' lists therefor shall be prepared in accordance with the laws of the province of Ontario in force for the purpose of the election of members to the assembly, but all persons entitled to vote hereunder may he named in said lists and those disentitled to vote shall not he named In said lists.
I trust that the Acting -Solicitor General will take the suggestions I have made into his very serious consideration.

I shall be glad
to have the attention of thS committee, particularly of the minister in charge of the Bill, while I ask that for a short time consideration be given to the question of the preparation of the voters' lists, from the point of view chiefly of the province of



Nova Scotia. I do not rise for the purpose of criticising the Bill or the action of the Government in the matter at all. I am giving my attention entirely to the making of suggestions which I hope may be found so reasonable that the minister can see the propriety of accepting them. At an earlier stage of the discussion of this measure I spoke of the desirability -of using the provincial lists as far as possible, and it is along that line that I wish to speak to the committee now. I suppose we can all admit that if the provincial lists are fair and reasonable, it would be well to have them adopted. The preparation of an electoral list is a matter of difficulty, a matter of expense, and a matter of trouble for the men who are interested in politics and sometimes where the political battle wages fiercely, it is a matter of considerable political strife. Now it is not desirable that these troubles and this strife shall he repeated if you can get from the province a fair list as a basis. Why should not that be adopted for Dominion purposes if it is a fair and reasonable list? I do not suppose there would be any dispute on that point.
There is an impression, I have gathered from conversations with some hon. members, and reference has been made to it in the IHfouse that the electoral list of Nova Scotia is largely a list based upon property qualifications. I want to point out that that is practically a mistake. There is a property qualification which is taken into consideration in preparing the original list, but it is not a fact that any man in Nova Scotia who ought to he entitled to vote is disqualified for -lack of property qualifications. The existing electoral law of Nova Scotia comes so near to the Dominion franchise that even if there were no change to be made in it, there would be no good reason for having separate lists.
T am going to ask the attention of the committee while I give them briefly a little history of the preparation of electoral lists and the creation of the franchise in Nova Scotia. There was a time, very long ago, when there was a property qualification, not a large one, but still a property qualification. Prior to 1863 theTe had been universal suffrage, what is now called manhood suffrage, but in that year the Government of the day brought in a Bill to adopt a restricted franchise. How that Bill came to he adopted, and what were its consequences on the political history of Nova Scotia, is a very interesting chapter, but does not concern us here. A re-

stricted franchise was adopted in 1863, and that remained the law without any material change until 1885. At that time I had the honour of being Prime Minister of the province, and it fell to my lot and was my privilege to introduce a Bill to widen the franchise by bringing in a very large proportion of the young men of the province. The new Bill proposed that the sons of farmers and sons living with their parents, if their property qualification either as owners or as yearly tenants was sufficient, should be brought in, and under that law the vast majority of the young men of the province were given the franchise in 1885, and that is a long time ago. At a later stage in our history there was added an income franchise, and when that franchise calling for an annual income of $250, I think, was added to the former we had a franchise so near to manhood suffrage that even if we took the provincial lists as they are to-day they would be practically the same as the Dominion lists prepared under this legislation. But there is to-day before the legislature of Nova Scotia a Bill introduced 'by a member of the Government and supported by the leader of the Opposition, and therefore likely to become law, to make the franchise of Nova Scotia correspond exactly with the Dominion franchise. I have already pointed out that even if there was no change made in the provincial law there would be no material difference, but that there may be no -room for difficulty on that score I point out to my hon. friends that this Bill introduced by a member of the Government and supported by the leader of the Opposition is now in process of passing through the legislature of Nova Scotia, and I take it for granted, for the reasons I have mentioned, that it will he enacted. So there will toe no difference between the franchise law of the Dominion and the franchise law of Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There are differences in the Bill. I have seen it.
Material differences?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There are differences,
but I understand there have been some amendments since I last saw the Bill.

I read only a newspaper report, and it stated that the object was to bring the Nova Scotia franchise substantially into harmony with the Dominion franchise. I have not had the Bill before me, but I take it for granted, having regard to the object of the legislation, that if there are any material differences, amendments

will be made, because I saw it stated by the minister introducing the Bill that the object sought was to conform with the Dominion franchise. Even if it were not so, the franchise law actually existing today is so near manhood suffrage that it is not worth while paying much attention to the difference, and I hope the minister will see that there is no reason why we should not adopt the Nova Scotia lists as they stand.
I am not going to move an amendment, but I shall read one which I have drafted, and leave it for the consideration of my hon. friend at a later moment. My object now is only to- assist in the discussion of this matter, and to give reasons why I think we ought not to have the two lists. My hon. friend (Mr. Boss) has given figures to show the enormous cost involved in preparing the lists, and I think that must be obvious to all. We will all surely agree that if the provincial lists are fair lists they ought to be adopted. Oot only for the convenience of the public, nor to save expense to the public treasury, but on both these grounds we should 'guard against having a repetition of the lists.
How are the Nova Scotia lists made up? There is an impression, I find, that there is some partisanship in the making up of the lists. That is not so, as far as I can learn. The lists are prepared by revisers appointed by the municipal councils, and I think it has come to be a very generally understood thing that men of both political parties are appointed to the revising board. The preliminary list is made up and published in all public places, and a day is fixed when those who are interested in the matter can apply to have a name added or a name struck off. On the day appointed they appear, and the lists are revised at that stage. Then there is a final stage; there is a court 'of appeal in the sheriffs of the province. I have heard it Suggested-I will not say argued, because it is no argument-that because the sheriffs are appointed by the Provincial Government, therefore they 'will be partisans. Let me repeat a suggestion I offered on a previous occasion. This Dominion Franchise Act assigns certain duties to the county judges. They are appointed by the Dominion Government. If I should object to that on the ground that because they are appointed by the Dominion Government they will therefore be partisan, that would be a very foolish argument. It would be no argument at all, nor is it any argument to say that the sheriffs of Nova Scotia because they are appointed by the Provin-1484
cial Government must be partisan. It so happens that nearly all the sheriffs in Nova Scotia are old and experienced public officials. Most of them are longer in the public service than any judges we have on the bench. There are eighteen sheriffs in Nova Scotia, sixteen of whom have held office for over five years, fifteen have held office for more than ten years, eight have held office for more than twenty years, and in my own constituency, where there are two sheriffs, one has been in office thirty-six years and the other forty-three years. These sheriffs are old and experienced officers, and although they imay have had their predilections, as we all have, before appointment, I submit that when men are appointed to public office- and I care not to what side they belong,- in nine cases out of ten they realize a sense of responsibility not to party -but to the state in which they are permanent officers. It is therefore but fair to say that men who have held the office of sheriff for all these years I have indicated are just as likely to be just and reasonable and nonpartisan as any judge of the Supreme Court or of the County Court of Nova Scotia, or any other province. I think that that is a fair argument, and I can see no answer for it. I urge that the fact that the appeal is to the sheriff of the province should not be regarded for a single moment as an indication that the sheriffs of this country will be partisan in this matter. I for one am confident that they will not be. It so happens that the Government of the province of Nova Beotia for a very long period has been Liberal, and inevitably they have appointed their friends. We do not blame them; we do not blame the Government of the day for appointing their friends to offices. It follows therefore that most of these men I have mentioned are Liberals, although in one case in my own county the sheriff is a Conservative. Whether they are Liberals or Conservatives, however, when such men, 'bein& good and worthy citizens, are appointed to responsible offices of this permanent character, they bring to their duties a sense of responsibility and justice and they should not be assumed to be partisans any more than the judges of the country are regarded as partisans because of the fact that at one time before they came to the Bench they had their own political preferences. The question of expense is a considerable one. My hon. friend from Middlesex has dealt with that question and has submitted certain figures. He says that there will not be much expense incurred in Ontario if

we adopt this proposal. Well, there will not be a dollar of expense -in Nova Scotia if you adopt what I suggest. The lists are always ready; they are revised every year, and you do not want any special lists. You can never have an election there without having a list ready, and if my suggestion were adopted it would not cost the Dominion of Canada one single penny. Why, then, should not lists of that kind be accepted as a finality? Why should lists made up in the way I have described be submitted to any one else in order that they may be added to or subtracted from? I do not discuss the question of motives or party at all in regard to this matter; I am simply stating the case from the point of view of common sense. The
5 p.m. motion I am about to read includes the province of New Brunswick, as I ata informed by my hon. friend from that province that the situation there is pretty much the same as in Nova Scotia. I will leave them, however, at a later stage to speak on the question from their point of view, but they assure me that the case of New Brunswick is very much like our own. I confine taiy remarks to Nova Scotia because I am best acquainted with conditions in that province and the suggestion I offer to the minister is that we insert a section 32jA the following:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in this Act, the lists of voters for the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick shall be those prepared and completed for the several polling divisions under the laws of the respective provinces for the purposes of provincial elections if they are completed within one year immediately preceding the issue of the writ for such election, and no names shall be added to or subtracted from such lists.
Now, I trust I have given the minister ample reason why he should not ask for any special lists in the province of Nova Scotia. I believe that there is no reason in the world why the lists prepared in the way I have described should not be accepted for Dominion purposes.

That is what I am getting at, and I have no doubt in the world that you will recognize that I will come around to it sooner or later. My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's now seems to be solicitous that every one should have the vote. Would I he out of order if I we e to recount, or retell, a little incident that occured in the local legislature between myself and the Premier of Nova Scotia? Murray, the successor of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, told me, as to the reason for this, that he knew not why, and I said to him across the floor:	" If you know not why,

Now my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) gets up and swells out his chest and talks about the honour and the honesty of politics. Ah, yes ! but when he was in power where was his honesty or integrity?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must point out to the hon. member that this committee is not dealing with the honesty and integrity of any member of it.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are discussing .a *certain clause, and the rule is clear that the discussion must be strictly relevant to that clause. I do hope that old political sores will not be raked over in the course of this discussion.
Bravo.

I know, Mr. Chairman,
that you are perfectly right, and you may have noticed that 1 have always bowed to the decision of the Chair. But let me go one little bit further and, I hope, not in a disorderly manner. Let me say this: That the first election that was run by the Laurier Government after its return to office, took place, if you remember, in 1901.

Very true, 1900. If you make search in the library yonder you will find that the previous year the statutes of Nova Scotia had been revised-and in that revision-one year before the election-entirely to my mind at the suggestion of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, George Murray, the Premier of Nova Scotia, had dropped from the statutes the Act that disqualified officials that were appointed by the Dominion Government. Now I ask you, gentlemen on both sides of this House, is it possible that sane men are going to take their standards from the member for Shelburne and Queen's? I won't.

I regret that I am
not able to agree with all of the statements which have been made by my hon. friend who represents the constituency of Shelburne and Queen's. I do not suppose for a moment that the hon. member intended to mislead the committee, but it really does seem to me that he could hardly have compressed more inaccuracies within the four corners of his speech if he had really set out with that object in view. I think therefore, Mr. Chairman, I will have to ask the, committee to bear with me while I go very briefly-if I can-into matters of a somewhat provincial character, in order to show exactly what the conditions in the province of Nova Scotia are as far as the revising of the lists is concerned. I am opposed to the proposition made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's

(Mr. Fielding) for various reasons. In the first place, the lists in the province of Nova Scotia, are, as he stated, revised by revisers appointed by the municipal councils. But unfortunately, for reasons which I will later explain, in that province the municipal councils are run on strictly party lines. Rural municipal elections-I do not now refer to municipal elections in cities and towns-are quite as partisan as are the Dominion and provincial elections. The result is that in every rural district partisans, or at least very strong party men, are elected to represent the various municipal districts. These men naturally appoint revisers whom they think will prepare lists which will make their re-election easy. I may say, so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, that I think that, with one or two exceptions, the party to which my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) belongs has control of all the municipal councils oif the province, which means that they have the appointment of all the revisers.
The councillors who appoint these revisers, as may be expected, are not men of quite the same stamp as members of the Provincial Legislature, and they are not quite as careful in their appointments as members of a larger and more influential body would be. I am speaking now of both Liberals and Conservatives. Consequently the revisers iare as a rule intense party men, They are not at all skilled in .the construction of statutes, they are just men picked up anywhere, without any particular knowledge of law, without any other qualification than the fact that they are capable supporters of the councillor from their district and may be depended upon to prepare a list favourable to his re-election. Into the hands of these laymen is placed a very complicated piece of legislation. I am not saying that it is designedly ambiguous, but I do say that there is not on the statute books of Nova Scotia a more ambiguous and difficult piece of legislation to construe than is the Franchise Act.
My hon. friend has said that there has been practically manhood suffrage in the province for a number of years. I am obliged to take very decided issue with him on that point. If he refers to the statutes of 1918 he will find two pages are covered in describing the -different franchise qualifications. A man may vote: if he owns $150 worth of real estate; if he owns $300 of real estate and personal property combined; if he rents a house or a piece of land worth $150; and there are various other qualifications. If a person owns $150 worth of real

estate in the province, whether he is a resident of his district or not, in the past he has been entitled to be registered as a voter. Moreover if a man is assessed for $150 worth of real estate on the municipal assessment roll, whether he is properly assessed or not, whether he owns any property or not, and whether he lives in the province or not, that qualifies him for a vote.
What has been the result of that legislation? It has led to the bedevilment of the assessment rolls. Unscrupulous assessors have in many instances loaded up the municipal assessment rolls with the names of men who are not owners of property, who are not residents in the province, but in many instances reside in the United States. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), if he will examine the assessment rolls of his own county, will, I am quite sure, find that condition of affairs there. I was unfortunate enough at one time to be connected with a by-election in my hon. friend's constituency, and I remember going very carefully over the lists and finding something like 400 nonresident voters in that county-persons with doubtful or no qualifications whatever, persons who were residing in the United States and who never came to the county except at election time, when they were brought over to deposit their ballots. I say that is a most vicious condition of affairs, and unfortunately that condition exists not only in my hon. friend's constituency but in almost every other constituency in that province.
But while there is no- residence qualification in so far as persons w!ho are assessed as property owners are concerned, there is a very rigid residential qualification in so far as persons voting-

If my
hon. friend will permit me. Does he say there is no residence qualification for voters in the province?

If my hon. friend had possessed his soul in patience a little while longer he would have found his question unnecessary; but I will answer it. I say that so far as persons who are assessed as owners of real estate of the qualifying amount are concerned, no residential qualification is required; but I do say that so far as other persons are concerned, there is a very exacting residential qualification required, and it is this

But my
hon. friend is aware that the Dominion Franchise Act requires a man to live in a constituency, and if the oath can be put to him, and he is on the list, that does not

affect the question at all, because the law that we are now passing contains a provision whereby that can be checked.

I think my hon. friend misses the point absolutely. The proposition, as I understand it from my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), is that we shall adopt the provincial lists, and that a person who is on the provincial lists shall be eligible to vote on a federal election.
That is all.

As I said before, if a
person does not happen to be assessed for property, if he is obliged to vote on his income qualification, he is surrounded with very strict provisions. Take, for example, the case of a clergyman, of a bank clerk, or of a commercial traveller-men who are changing their residence very frequently; they find under the law of the province that - they are debarred from voting. The residential qualification is something like this: A man must be a resident of the county in which he is to vote for one year from the first day of January preceding the day of the revision of the lists. The lists are revised on the fifth of March. If therefore a clergyman moves into my county on the 2nd of January, 1920, he cannot be registered on the 5th March, 1920, because he has not been in the county a year; more than that, he cannot be registered in 1921 because he has not been a resident of the county for a year from the 1st January preceding the date of revision. The list made up in 1921 holds good until the middle of April, 1922. Consequently that clergyman could not vote if an election was held before the middle of April, 1923. Now, my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) dwelt very pathetically the other day upon the awful sense of injustice and wrong which would rankle in the heart of the child of a woman who, under the clause that was put through the other night, would, by reason of her alien birth, have to go before a judge to get a certificate in order that she might be enabled to vote. If we were to adopt the proposal of the member for Shelburne -and Queen's, what would be the position of the clergyman's child, who, when election day came around, found that all the dishonourable thugs in the community had a vote while -he, whose father was a leader in spiritual matters in the community, was debarred? 'I object to that proposition.

My hon. friend is

A man iwho is exempt from assessment certainly is not assessed, and the law says that a man must be assessed for $250 income 'before he can vote on that qualification. [DOT]who oocu<py pulpits do not receive that remuneration, although in almost every case they deserve much more.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Is there a special clause in regard to clergymen or ministers, or does the same rule apply to all?

The same rule applies to all; I am just citing the clergymen as an instance. The same applies to a bank manager, to a school teacher, to the hundred and one different occupations engaged in by people who frequently have occasion to change their places of residence. Then, ft must be remembered that the list is closed on the tenth day of April and if an election comes say the next February, under the proposal of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) the voter would be voting on lists almost a year old. That would mean that intelligent men, men occupying high positions, who have lived in 'the district for four years, would be debarred from the right to vote.
, Now, my hon. friend said that an appeal to the sheriff makes for a fair list; that a sheriff is just as good a man as a county court judge. I take very decided issue with him there. There is a great difference between a county court judge and a sheriff. For many years the Opposition in Nova Scotia have asked the Government to amend the law so that an appeal would lie to a county court judge. There are seven county court judges in Nova Scotia; four were [DOT]appointed by the party to which my hon. friend belongs, and three 'by either the Liberal-Conservative party or the Union Government. The Nova Scotia Government refused point-blank to permit an appeal to the county court judge; they insisted upon an appeal to the sheriff,-who, my hon. friend says, is [DOT] an absolutely independent, capable officer. My hon. friend will admit that the sheriff is not as well versed in the law as is the county court judge. The minimum salary of a sheriff in Nova Scotia is, I think, $700; you can readily understand that a salary of that kind does not attract the most acute legal minds in the province. An appeal lies from the three laymen revisers to the layman sheriff. The sheriff is in an entirely different position from that of the county court judge. The county court judge has a knowledge of law; the sheriff is usually a man who was acting as constable or something of that kind and, because of his political proclivities, made himself so useful to the party in power that he was appointed to the more remunerative and more honourable position of sheriff. That is the

kind of men who were appointed. I admit that the sheriffs in Nova Scotia are of a very much better class than they were when my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) was Premier of that province. But they are far from being men who have judicial minds. They get their inspiration and their advice from the Attorney General of the province. In cases of dispute the sheriffs feel bound to take the advice of the Attorney General,-and right there I want to relate just a little incident which will illustrate my point and give you some insight into the condition of affairs in Nova Scotia.
In 1911, I as prospective candidate for the provincial legislature, took a good deal of interest in the revising of the lists. I organized my county as best I could, and had the interests of my parts fairly represented'before the revisers. Following that I fought the thing out before the sheriff of the county; we looked after the technicalities and did the work as well as we could. Under the law the sheriff is obliged to file his list with the county clerk, on the tenth day of April, I think,-anyway, the date is not material. I made a point of being at the municipal clerk's office the day that the sheriff was to file his list. I looked it over and found that apart altogether from appeals, apart altogether from cases which were legally brought before him, the sheriff had, by striking off without cause the names of my friends and putting on the names of political opponents, made a net change in the list to the tune of 193 votes. I called by telephone the Attorney General, who was then the Hon. A. K. Maclean, and explained that this thing was an outrage and that it must he stopped. Mr. Maclean agreed that it must be stopped and finally he promised that he would wire the sheriff to make a correction and to see that this scandal was not carried out.
Will the hon. member state what was the year in which that happened?

In April, 1911. If my hon. friend wants any confirmation of my story, I refer him to the member for Halifax (Hon. A. K. Maclean). Although I have no word from the then Attorney General to substantiate my statement, I believe that he was as good as his word. I did observe afterwards a messenger from the telegraph office deliver a telegram to the sheriff, who was then in the clerk's office. The clerk afterwards informed me that when the sheriff got the message he left

the office and went to the office of Hon. O. T. Daniels, then provincial member for the county. After spending a little time with Mr. Daniels the sheriff returned to his office and said: "Mr. Daniels says this thing is all right; I am going to put this list through just as it is."
Mr. Daniels, who was then provincial member for the county and who afterwards became Attorney General for the province of Nova Scotia, is the man who would be the final court of appeal on these federal lists if the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) were agreed to.

Is this same Mr. O. T.
Daniels, Attorney General of Nova Scotia, the man whose picture figured in the Police Gazette in New York?

I am always glad to
answer any question of my hon. friend, but perhaps this question is not relevant to the subject under consideration. I can, however, satisfy him outside.
I am right, am I?

As I said before, I
could multiply cases of this character, but I do not think that is necessary. I have dealt so far only with the law as it formerly was. I am now going to deal for a moment or two with the proposition as amended. It is a most extraordinary thing that for years and years the Opposition in the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia has been trying to get the Provincial Government to abolish the fictitious qualifications of the old Act and to adopt manhood suffrage. That was not accomplished until within the last few weeks when a measure was introduced into the provincial legislature, and the hon. member (Mr. Fielding) who is endeavouring to steer this amendment through, seems to know all about the matter. I do not want to ibe suspicious; but it looks to me almost as though there was a guilty knowledge between these two gentlemen and that the scheme in Nova Scotia was part of the scheme as we have seen it attempted in this House to-day. However that may be, my hon. friend is very much in error in reference to the contents of this Bill and its success in getting through the House. As a matter of fact, the Bill, as introduced into the provincial legislature, is decidedly different in many Tespects, which I may have occasion to point out later on in this debate, from the Bill which is at present before this House. I am going to point out just one or t?W0' striking differences. In the first place, the Bill that we are discussing to-day provides that any
person who is a British subject, who is a resident of Canada for one year and a resident of the polling district in which he desires to vote, for two>
months preceding the election, is qualified to be registered. That is the only qualification. In Nova Scotia, the qualification is very different. The Act as it passed in the provincial legislature requires that the applicant must be a resident of the county of which the polling district forms a part for one year previous to the first day of January last past. Therefore, this is open to exactly the objections I have stated before in reference to the old Act. It is even worse than that, because by the affidavit which the applicant is obliged to take, his residence is confined not only to the county, but to the polling district itself. Let ine read the affidavit which it is necessary for a man to make if he wishes to have his name added to the voters' list.
I,	solemnly swear:
1.	That I am (or he or she is) a British subject by birth or naturalization of the full age of twenty-one years.
2.	That I am and have been (or he or she is
and has been) a resident of the province of Nova Scotia for at least one year next before the first day of January last and so resided in polling district No.	in the county of
during said period.
That means that before a man can vote under the Nova Scotia Act as amended, he must actually foe a resident of the polling district from one year from the first day of January preceding the date of the revision. That, at one stroke, would practically disqualify, I believe, fully one-quarter of the total electorate of the province of Nova Scotia. That is the kind of a list which my hon, friend suggests that this House should adopt.
My particular reason against this House adopting any municipal or provincial list is this, that I believe it will have a tendency to introduce federal politics into municipal affairs, and that I consider would be an outrage. The criticism is raised and, I fear with too much force, that we residents of Nova Scotia are a bit partisan in our nature. That certainly applies to hon. members opposite from Nova Scotia; I do not know whether it applies to members on this side of the House. It is, to some extent, true that we in Nova Scotia take, perhaps, too extreme political views on public questions. I believe the secret of the whole thing is in the system inaugurated by my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding), which he would try to induce this committee to perpetuate. When my hon. friend became premier of Nova Scotia as a very shrewd and astute

politician, he decided that he must have control of the lists. Therefore he went to work to capture every municipal council in Nova Scotia.. I do not condemn him for that; I think his action was wise. He said: We must have a list favourable to ourselves and so we must have municipal councils in sympathy with and of the same stripe as the Government. The result was that he introduced a vein of party politics into municipal affairs, and that has been there ever since. That is a curse. When the people of a municipality are called upon to elect a councillor, they should not ask the question whether he be a Unionist or a Liberal; they should inquire only into his personal qualifications. Furthermore, when a municipal council appoints a man to prepare the assessment rolls, it should have no regard whatever for his political proclivities. But if we are going to put the question of revision of the lists for federal purposes into the hands of these men, by that very act we make partisans of them; we introduce the curse of party politics into municipal affairs. I certainly entertain a strong conviction that this House will not consider any proposal such as that.

I should like to say a few words in reference to the electoral list of New Brunswick. I shall certainly ask the Government to adopt this list because I believe, on account of the way in which it is prepared, it is as perfect a list as can be made in the whole Dominion. From what I can understand as regards making up the lists throughout Canada, I believe New Brunswick is, I shall not say ahead of any other province, but equal to any other province. The list is a perfect one because it is acceptable without any complaints from either political party, and' if any other hon. member from New Brunswick is present, he will bear me out in that statement. This list is prepared by a very independent board of revisers. This board is composed of one gentleman appointed by the Provincial Government, who is the chairman, and two others who are appointed by the electors of each parish of a county. In this way the councillors when they are elected are revisers. They are the choice of the people from each and every parish. This board of revisers meets in September, I think, of each year and prepares a list of the voters, which is posted up in every public place in the province. A new list is made every year. After making the list, notice is given that the board will sit one month later, before which applicants can be heard as to the

adding of names to the list or striking them off. When this has been done by the board in November, the lists are filed with the county secretary, who makes a copy of the lists filed from every parish and every county of the province. He then notifies the sheriffs of the counties who go over the lists with him to see that they are true copies. The sheriff then certifies the list, putting his name on every page. There you have the official list for .the county, and on the first of January of each year these lists come into force and are available in case of an election being held throughout the year.
As to qualifications, we have manhood suffrage in New Brunswick. A man twenty-one years of age, whether he owns property or not, has the right to vote. We have also extended the franchise to women on the same basis. I think by the method I have described we get a perfect list. I have handled the lists many times myself, and I have never received a complaint from any candidate or any man belonging to either one party or the other, that the lists were not right. They are as perfect as they can be made, and I would therefore urge the minister to accept these provincial lists as the basis for the Dominion lists. I think every member of this House from the province of New Brunswick, no matter on which side he sits, will admit that the lists are as perfect as they can be made.

Ten of those elections were conducted under the system of franchise which we are advocating in regard to the making of lists, and only three were held under the system of registration or revising barristers as the case may be. When the Dominion of Canada came into being as such Sir John Macdonald, who I suppose had most to do with the drafting of the British North America Act, put into that Act the provision that until a franchise was prepared by the Dominion Parliament, the local lists in each province should be used. That arrangement continued absolutely satisfactory, as far as I know, to both Liberals and 'Conservatives down to the year 1885, when the Revising Barristers Act wras put through this Parliament after a very strenuous fight and the crossing of swords by such gladiators as Sir John Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, Hon. Edward Blake, Sir Richard Cartwright, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and other men of that calibre who debated the question

further on the subject except that I hold my hon, friend (Mr. Butts) responsible for the doings of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's during the years that the latter -was Prime Minister of Nova Scotia because he supported him in his every action.
There has been a great deal of talk to the effect that we are not entitled to have the privilege of preparing those lists 'because for ninety years we were taking certain officials off the lists in Nova Scotia. That is a matter which dates back earlier than the administration of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's, and since nobody seems to have given light on that point I will touch upon it very briefly, because we are told that because of the facts of history and of the partiality that is alleged to have been displayed in the past we in the province of Nova Scotia should not be given the power to prepare our own lists. It is well known that Nova Scotia was forced into Confederation absolutely against her will. In 1867 there was a general election in the province of Nova Scotia, and out of a Dominion representation of eighteen or twenty members one solitary man, the late Sir Charles Tupper, was returned to this House on the Confederation [DOT]issue. In the local legislature only two men [DOT]were returned on that issue, their names [DOT]being Blanchard and Pineo, and the names [DOT]of these three men will go down in history. That was the feeling of Nova Scotia in 1867 against Confederation into which the province was forced without the people being consulted. There was such a furore against anything from Ottawa that the Government of that day passed an Act that officials of the Departments of Customs and Railways- those were the only two departments selected, why I do not know-should not be allowed to vote. Of course, that law did not apply to the Dominion franchise. It was allowed to remain on the statute hook for years, and the Tory party when in power in 1872 and again in 1882 did not attempt to repeal it. I am proud to be able to say that in 1900 I had the honour of introducing into the legislature of Nova Scotia, .for the first time as far as I know, the Bill that repealed this disability. That Bill passed the Legislative Assembly but was defeated in the Council, but later it was re-introduced and passed both Houses. To cast this up to the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) is absurd, for he had nothing whatever to do with that disability. He was not in politics until many years after that Act was put on the statute books.

I have only to say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that the exercise of the local franchise for fifty-three years with only one single solitary case of irregularity is a fairly good record. We have 18 counties in the province and several cities and incorporated towns, but the only single report of anything irregular in those fifty-three years is the case that comes to us from the county of Annapolis. I venture to tell my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) that if he had made complaint to the Premier of Nova Scotia an investigation would have been ordered at once, and the sheriff he speaks of would have been removed if found to have been remiss in his duty.
The extreme partisanship that has been referred to does not exist in Nova Scot*a. For fourteen years I was a member of the municipal council of my town; five of those years I was mayor; and all through the fourteen years, although we had a strong Liberal majority in the council, we had three good Tory revisers. Does not that prove to my good friend from Regina that we are not the outlaws he thinks we are, refusing to give any one an appointment unless he pronounces the shibboleth of Liberalism or something akin to it?
With the exception of the interval between 1887 and 1898, for over forty years we have had in Nova Scotia an absolutely local franchise, and nothing can be brought against its administration except one single questionable case. I think that that record justifies us in asking that we be left with a system in which we have absolute confidence. If any other province wants different lists, well and good; we do not want to interfere. All we want is to retain what we were promised by the memorandum that was handed to me and what we are accustomed to. I hope no such-mistake will be made as to tear apart every list we have and commence a new list which cannot by any possibility be satisfactory, under a system with which we are not acquainted and for the preparation of which there will not be sufficient time.
Carried.

I will gratify my hon. friend in a few minutes. But if any hon. gentleman thinks that we are so kaiserized in this House that it is an offence for me to make these remarks let me assure him that I do not propose to be deprived of the liberty of speaking for my people because some hon. gentleman who has had his mind made up for him shouts "carried." That gentteman will have to settle with the hon.

member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham), who has told us that some hon. members have no minds to make up because everything is settled for them. I shall cling tenaciously to our British parliamentary procedure and put my case before the House. If hon. gentlemen on the other side do not agree with me, that is their privilege under constitutional majority rule; but let me assure them that as there was of old an appeal to Caesar, so there will be an appeal to Caesar in this case.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
heard for the first time from my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) that some solemn pledge and undertaking was given to him by some members of this Government prior to the passage of the ByElections Act one or two sessions ago.

I have the original
document here which I can pass over to my hon. friend.
Mr. GUTHRIE.: I would like very much to see the document. I must inform the committee that up till the moment my hon. friend spoke I was in entire ignorance of the existence of such a document.
The document has now been handed to me by my hon. friend. It is headed, as I assumed it would be:
Proposals for the Creation of a Franchise Act for the Purpose of holding By-elections until after the next Session of Parliament.
It does not appear to be dated, but I have no doubt that it was prior to the passage of the By-elections Act. The committee will pardon me if I read it; it is all new to me:
1.	The proposed legislation is contingent upon a public announcement by the Prime Minister to the House of Commons that he will not advise His Excellency the Governor General to dissolve Parliament until after another session has been held.
2.	Complete demobilization under the Wartimes Election Act shall be in effect on August 1st, 1919, and the Election Law as it stood prior to the War-times Election Act then to be brought into force with such amendments as may be absolutely necessary to meet changed conditions, including:-	.
(a)	The creation of machinery by which the names of women qualified to vote can be placed upon lists where none such now exist, e.g., New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario.
(b)	The adoption of existing permanent lists,
if any exist, in the respective provinces to which the women's names have been added. This probably applies to Nova Scotia and British Columbia.	.	,
(c)	The creation of machinery whereby lists can be created so that an election could be held within thirty days in any province where lists are not now complete, the most outstanding example being the province of Ontario,
where no lists exist, as a new law was passed in 1917, and no lists so far have been prepared under the law.
(d)	Where it is necessary either to make new lists or to add to the existing lists, that the principles of the local law of the province of Saskatchewan be adopted, which generally are as follows:-
Personal registration in cities and incorporated towns with a right of appeal to the County Court or District Judge and enumeration in rural committees, with the right to any person to swear in his or her vote on election day, in case the name has been omitted from the list made up by the enumerators, no ballots to be
tied up.	. .	,
(e)	Wherever officials, either municipal or provincial, now exist whose duty it is to prepare provincial voters' lists these officials should be appointed enumerators for the purpose of making the necessary additions.
