(f)	No person of foreign birth, male or female, to have the franchise unless personally naturalized.	.
(g)	A Public Prosecutor to be appointed in each constituency whose duty it will be to prosecute all persons who falsely swear their names upon a list or swear in a vote.
(h)	This Act to continue for the purpose of by-elections until March 1st, 1920, unless previously superseded by a general franchise Act.
What is wrong with that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I take it from
the heading that it was a proposal; for it is headed " Proposals for the Creation of a Franchise Act for the purpose of holding By-elections. until after the next session of Parliament."

And to be continued
into the new Act. That is not written there, but that is the intent of it.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen may
laugh, hut I am not afraid of their laughter.0 That was the statement that was given to me by two ministers. It would be quite like them not to stand by it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The first observation 1
have to make is that my hon. friend refers to this as a solemn pledge and undertaking by the Government which he accepted. Well, I think there must be some misunderstanding on the part of my hon. friend if he accepted that proposal, which distinctly says, in paragraph (f):
No person of foreign birth, male or female, to have the franchise unless personally naturalized.
If my hon. friend accepted that proposal, I cannot understand the speech he made a night or two ago. I think I am right when I say that this was really a proposal; it was to be the basis of a discussion between the Government and my hon. friend,

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: who was then the leader of the Opposition. But it could not in any sense of the word be regarded as a solemn pledge and undertaking which he accepted; otherwise he would never have made the speech he did the other night upon the question of the naturalization of aliens.

If the minister will
permit me, he may think that clever-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, I do not think it
clever.

The speech I made in
reference to the By-election Act was quoted here the night before last. If my hon. friend will do me the honour of reading the quotation he will see that I said: For the present we will accept this, holding to ourselves absolutely the right to criticize any franchise proposals that may be brought down; preserving all our rights intact. My speech was quoted the other night by the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and my hon. friend can see it at any time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That may be all right. The point I make is that the document I have now read must, from its very nature, have been a proposal in regard to the Byelections Act and not in regard to the general Elections Act. If this is a solemn pledge and undertaking by the Government which he accepted-that is his own language-as the basis of a general election Act or as a basis of the present Act, then my hon. friend accepted an agreement in regard to the franchise for aliens entirely contrary to the opinions which he expressed in this House two or three nights ago. I think I am right in assuming that this document which I have just read referred only to the By-elections Act, and formed only what it says it is, "proposals" as to what legislation should be enacted in respect to by-elections. Now, I want to have a chance to confer with my colleagues in regard to the matter. I may be wrong, but from the circumstances and from the language of the document I think I am right in assuming that it was purely and simply a basis of discussion for the then proposed By-election Act and had nothing to do with the permanent Act. But if I find, after discussing the matter with my colleagues, that I am wrong, I shall be quite glad to say so.
My hon. friend also, during the course of his remarks, in discussing the merits of the Voters' Act of Nova Scotia, referred to a statement made in this House in 1894 [Mr. Guthrie. 1
by the late Sir John Thompson, when he expressed the opinion that the franchises in existence in the various provinces had become so nearly alike that there was not much object in maintaining distinctions as between federal and provincial franchises. Sir John Thompson certainly did make that statement. But he made another statement immediately afterwards which my hon. friend failed to read. Sir John Thompson said we could not continue any distinctions in regard to franchises, but he said also-this is on the same page of Hansard:
The great principle which underlay the Franchise Act of 1885 was the control by this Parliament over matters connected with the franchise. .	.	. We adhere to the principle
that this House and the electors who return members to this House ought not to be under the control as regards the exercise of their franchise of the officers of any other Government or Legislature whatever in the country.
That is the point that we are trying to maintain in the present Bill. My hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) discussed the question of provincial franchise and provincial voters' lists this afternoon and offered a suggestion which he said he would later in the proceedings move as an amendment. His object in stating the purport of the 'amendment at this time was that the Government might have an opportunity of considering it before coming to a conclusion. The suggested amendment was long and somewhat involved, and I would like to have an opportunity of giving it careful study before pronouncing upon it. But as I understand from my hon. friend's reading of it, it involves our accepting in Ontario as final and complete the provincial voters' lists of that province provided they are not more than a year old and that any names which might .be added to those lists or taken from them should be so added to ot taken from them by a board appointed by the Ontario Government for that purpose. That system is not very different from the system laid down in clause 32 of the Bill. Clause 32 provides that provincial lists shall be accepted, shall be the lists, where they are not more than twelve months old. If the provincial lists in Ontario are more than twelve months old, we must have new lists. The Ontario franchise and the Dominion franchise are not exactly alike; there are differences. I was very familiar with these differences a short time ago, but I have had so many franchise Acts in my head lately, that I cannot express a positive opinion at

the present time as regards the provincial Act. There were differences between the last provincial Franchise Act and the present proposals of the Government. The differences were not radical, it is true. There were differences in the requirement as to residence and matters of that kind; there were differences, I think, as regards the disqualification of Indians; there was a difference as regards the disqualification of officials. Then the Ontario Voters' List Act which is now in force differs radically from this proposal. There is a proposal before the Ontario legislature at the present time, but I do not know whether it will be carried in the form in which it was introduced or not. I know that in the preparation of that Bill the Ontario Government had the advantage of reading the proposed Dominion Bill and in many instances followed our clauses, but in many other cases they did not follow our clauses. The only practical difference as regards lists between what the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. Boss) proposes and what this Bill proposes is this, that provided the Ontario list is not more than twelve months' old, under clause 32 of the present Bill names may be added to the list or struck from the list by a court designated by this Parliament, whereas under the provincial law this is done by a board composed of the county judge and some other individuals. I am not sure, for the moment, who compose the board, and I see the hon. member (Mr. Ross) who has a copy of the Bill, is not in his seat. As I have no copy of the Bill, I would like a little more time to consider that matter further. IBut the difference between the two proposals is not very great.
iMr. McOOIG: Provided that the Ontario lists have been revised in certain counties and not in others, would the lists be used in a Dominion election in counties in which the lists had been revised and would they not be used in counties in which the lists had not been revised?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 32 reads:
For the purposes of any Dominion election held within the limits of a province the voters' lists shall, except as hereinafter provided, he those prepared and completed for the several polling divisions, under the laws of that province, within one year immediately preceding the issue of the writ for such election.
Yes, I think they would.
Is there any special reason for making the lists revised within one year?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
So many changes take place after a list is one year old that it cannot be relied on; it is considered old or stale, and that is the object of having a one-year limitation. In answer to my hon. friend (Mr. MoCoig), I may say that in any riding in Ontario where there is a list which can be legally used for any election in Ontario and which is not more than one year old from the date of revision to the date of the issue of the writ, under this Bill that list will be the list for the Dominion election, and if names are omitted from it which should be added or if names should be stricken from it, the machinery is provided by this clause whereby that end may be attained. The question is-shall that end be attained by the machinery provided by clause 32, or shall it be attained by the procedure provided by the proposal of the Ontario Legislature when that proposal becomes law? It is important, as Sir John Thompson pointed out in 1894, that the House recognize the principle that it should control the individuals who have charge of the revision and completion of these lists. Apart from that single distinction, there is not very much in the proposal of the hon. member (Mr. Ross) which does not appear in clause 32 at the present moment. If we take the case where there is no provincial list that is not more than twelve months old, what does the hon. member propose to do in that case? If our provincial voters' lists are more than a year old, they cannot be used. I assume if such a thing should happen-and it has happened in Ontario-we would then be driven back to the provisions of clause 32 in its entirety.
Just a word now as regards the suggestion of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) regarding the provincial voters' lists of Nova Scotia. There is perhaps greater objection on his side of the House to the proposal to accept as final and complete the lists of the province of Nova Scotia in regard to the lists of the province of Ontario. Rightly or wrongly, I gather only from what I hear from others, there exists on this side of the House a feeling amongst hon. gentlemen who represent constituents in Nova Scotia, .that the lists of that province are not as absolutely fair as my hon. friends from that province who sit opposite to me would have the committee believe. This may be a difference of opinion only; but certainly there is a deep-rooted feeling amongst hon. members on this side of the House from Nova Scotia that the .provincial lists are not

fair to them and are generally unsatisfactory. I state that because it is a feeling that exists and that must be recognized. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) goes further than my hon. friend (Mr. Ross); he says that the Government should accept an amendment which would provide that the lists, as finally revised in Nova Scotia by the provincial authorities, shall be final; in other words, that the Government, in passing its own Franchise Act, its own election law, should be bound by lists prepared by officials of another government, at the present moment not on altogether friendly terms towards this Government. The main objection that has been urged upon me by hon. members with whom I have discussed the question is this, that at the present moment the only valid Voters' List Act in Nova IScotia is one involving a property qualification. There is at the present moment before the legislature of Nova Scotia a proposal to make their franchise generally upon the basis of the proposed Dominion franchise. Whether that Bill will be passed or not and in what form it will be passed, I cannot offer a prediction; but in a copy of the Bill which I had the privilege of reading, I found some distinctions as regards residence, and some as regards other matters which have escaped my mind. But it is purely problematical what the Bill will actually be when it becomes law. The present Voters' List Act of Nova Scotia would not agree with ours at all. The requirements are entirely different. My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) minimizes the property requirements under the present law in Nova Scotia but they are there, and they apply to man and to woman. That would not meet our Franchise Act in any respect. When the Act now pending before the legislature becomes law one might be able to form some opinion as to whether they meet us upon common ground in regard to the franchise; perhaps not identically the same ground, but approximately the same ground. We might then discuss whether or not we could to some extent or to any extent adopt the provincial lists in Nova Scotia. For my own part-I cannot speak for my colleagues because I have not had an opportunity of discussing this proposal with them-I would hesitate to adopt those lists as final and complete, and I will give the reasons that strike me. The appeal in the province of Nova Scotia is to the sheriff. Except in Scotland, I never heard of an appeal to the sheriff, and in Scotland the sheriff is a judicial officer.

Why the appeal to the sheriff in Nova Scotia, I do not know.

Because we have
eighteen counties in Nova Scotia and only seventeen county court judges. It was the only alternative. An appeal to the judges would not have met the convenience of the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That may be the reason, but it does not strike me as a very good one. Sheriffs in the province of Ontario as far as I know, are not lawyers. I do not know a single sheriff in the province that ever was a lawyer, and I think from what my horn, friend (Mr. Davidson) has said, that it is so in Nova Scotia. I do not know whether they have any qualifications to decide a legal point, and certainly legal judgment is necessary in deciding these appeals. I have been told that time and again it has been urged on the Government of Nova Scotia to allow the appeals to be decided toy the county court judges, and time and again that request has been refused. I think it is an objection to the system that the final decision rests with the sheriff.
But there is a far greater objection than that. In Ontario the sheriff is an officer accountable to1 the Attorney General's department and when the sheriff in Ontario wants advice he communicates with the Attorney General's department. I fancy the same system is in vogue in Nova Scotia. If a sheriff hearing an appeal is in doubt, he calls up the Attorney General. Now the Attorney General is certainly a very much interested individual, and if his voice is to govern, I think it might he termed a partisan voice. I think-this is only my own judgment-'that that system is defective, and I would not be disposed to ask the Government to accept a proposal of that kind unless better machinery for the hearing of these appeals was provided for. That would appeal to me to toe reasonable, and I trust it strikes the committee as reasonable too.
The only difference, then, between the Bill as drawn and the suggestion of my hon. friend this afternoon is this; The Bill as drawn says that in the province of Nova Scotia we shall accept the provincial lists if they are not more 'than twelve months old, and there shall toe power to add names to the list or strike names off it. In the cities and towns that will be before the judge, and in the rural districts before the rural registrar. If he acts improperly and strikes your name off the list we have put in the safeguard that on polling day you

can go and cast your vote upon taking the necessary oath, and you -will not be asked to put in what is known as a tied ballot. That proposal always has appeared to me to be a reasonable one. There is no way of depriving a man of a vote under the machinery provided in section 32. If a man wants to vote and is entitled to vote, there is no iway of depriving him of his vote. That, I think, is something in advance of any electoral Act we have had in this country before.
When we come to section 63 of this Act, which has been allowed to stand as dependent on section 32, I propose to move an amendment to safeguard the right which we give to an elector to vote on election day. The amendment is to this effect: That the elector must bring forward two resident ratepayers of the polling division who will vouch for him, who will take an oath that they know him and know that he is entitled to vote. I am proposing to add that since the Bill was introduced. It will leave the matter this way: that any man in a rural division who is left off the list through the evil mind or ill disposition of any official of the Government can go to the polls on polling day and claim the right to vote. He must 'bring with him two resident ratepayers of that division who are willing to swear that he is entitled to vote. He has also to swear it himself. His name is entered in the poll book with the names of his two bondsmen, and I do not think you will find in any rural division of this country three men who will perjure themselves for the sake of a single vote. I think that safeguard is almost absolute. In the city divisions the procedure is different. There we allow an appeal, and the appeal goes to the judge. If in large centres there may be more appeals than a single judge can attend to, we do not appoint an appellate court even, but the judge himself designates other persons, not necessarily judges, to form an appellate court. If my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) Nvill reconsider his own suggestion and will take from it those words " final and complete " he will find that my views very largely coincide with his, and I think the section is going to work out very largely as he desires if we leave it just as it is. I understand from hon. members from Nova Scotia that the lists there are prepared annually. We can safely say, then, that an election would fall within that twelve-month limitation, and under section 32 we would then be bound to accept that list. We will be saving the expense of making a new list. Then we provide as simple machinery as possible
to allow people to have their names added to the list, and opportunity is given to have names struck off. This is carried on by officers designated in the Act, and I think it is as fair a way as anybody could suggest,
I see the difficulty pointed out by my hon. friend (Mr. Davidson). I have heard it discussed by at least half a dozen members from Nova Scotia. To us in Ontario it seems little short of an outrage that by any possibility a man may have to wait three or four years before he can vote. If it so happens that he moves into a district on the 2nd of January, instead of before the 1st of January, he may be kept there almost indefinitely before he has a legal right to get on the list. My hon. friend from Lunenburg says: We strain the law a little in a case of that kind and we put these people on. But that is not the legal way of doing the thing. I was told by another member, and a high authority too, that on account of these peculiar dates that are adopted in the Nova Scotia law, a man may actually be twenty-three before he can vote, instead of having the right to vote at twenty-one. They may continue these restrictions if they like, hut I repeat, we must accept their list if it is not twelve months old. We are not going to allow, however, any class of people to be disqualified on account of difficulties of that kind with regard to duties; these people can have their names added under this section. There is an objection to what my hon. friend speaks of as municipal and provincial lists. We find it every day in the province of Ontario. Every man who is assessed is entitled to have his name on the list, and it is always difficult at election time to strike off the non-residents, and in large cities there are on the voters' lists the names of a great many people who are not legally entitled to vote. Men happen to own property but do not live in the division, and there is a great opportunity in the larger centres for what is known as "plugging." A man comes along whom nobody knows; he says "I am So-and-So," and no one can refute the statement, and he votes in the name of some non-resident. This cannot be done in rural districts and smaller towns where practically everybody knows everybody else. In the larger cities, however, it has been practised extensively in the past, and this is a matter for the consideration of my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross).

May I draw the minister's attention to the fact that non-residents are always put in part 3 of the list?

Mir. 'GUTHRIE:	I can show my hon.
friend lists of last year where I can find twenty names of people non-resident in the division.
Possibly they have moved away.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A man is on the list today and he moves away to-morrow and his name remains, and that is what I object to. In a county such as my hon. friend represents, and in my own county, every one knows every one else pretty much, but in such places as London, Hamilton and Toronto we know that plugging has been carried on extensively by reason of the fact that names of non-resident electors appeared on the list. When the plugger comes along no one can dispute his right to 'vote; he casts his vote and away he goes.

That would be possible
under any circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not under a list prepared here within forty days of the poll; you can strike off or add to it at any time. One of the chief advantages of this law is the fact that it will give an up-to-date list, and so far as I can see that list will be an absolutely non-partisan one. I do not see any ground for all the fears expressed by my hon. friend from West Middlesex, who must be nervous or must have qualms of conscience. Unless you begin on the assumption that every one is crooked I do not see what objection there can be to the law.

The minister says that a
lot of plugging has been practised. Well, that can go on under any conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not under this law.
This will not prevent personation.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Actually the list will
not be more than two or three weeks old when it is voted on, and any unknown names will be stricken off. Non-resident voters will go off and the names of those who should be on the list will be added. You will have an up-to-date list, a list prepared almost up to nomination day. It will be a last-minute list. There might be an exceptional case where an unknown man might work in.
How many cases of plugging does the minister know of in his constituency? As a matter o-f fact there has been little plugging, and I think that the minister is exaggerating in that respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I should not like to give the -source of my information, but we have strong reasons foT believing that in 18% we lost the election in my riding
10 p.m. through plugging. I will tell my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee), when he puts his innocent question in that bland manner of his, that I could not teach him anything about the matter.
Well, I do not know what the minister means by that assertion, I am sure; but if he implies that I have ever been guilty of anything unfair, I desire to inform him that he is absolutely wrong.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You asked me the question.
I simply asked the minister how much plugging there had been, and when he says that he cannot teach me anything, I can only say that evil minds conceive what ought not to be thought of.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I do not like any assumption of innocence in this matter.
Nobody does.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We have been long
enough in politics to know what the records of the courts are.
You need not impute any plugging to me; I do not know anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You know as much as I do.

Then God knows you
know nothing, so far as that is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, we are on even
ground.

I think it comes with
very bad grace from the minister to make such insinuations.
Order.
It is in very bad taste.

Order;
I must point out that the minister has the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If the discussion in
this direction goes any further I can also refer to the instance of the London election when-
Well?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-an election was stolen from the Liberal party in 1887 by plugging;

and I know the experience in South Wellington in 1896. We always thought we lost the election by plugging by reason of the fact that the non-resident vote in those days was allowed, and the voters' list was full of names of non-residents whom we could not locate.
Does the minister connect me with anything of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I made my remark in
perfect innocence, and thought it would be accepted in that way.

I take it that way then.
Mr. G'UTHRIE:	I hope the indignation
has passed away.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
To get back to the
clause, Mr. Chairman, I say that the safeguards provided in this clause are the most complete that I have ever come across in an Election Act. I do not believe that a band of crooked election officials could deprive a man of his vote under this law if he wanted to vote. If he were deprived it would be because of his own carelessness. I do not want to see any objection in either of the proposals that have been suggested. I do not object to them except in regard to the machinery they propose in the way of appeal. I think we should provide for the Appellate Court here. If my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's will think the matter out a little further I think he will agree with me in that respect. Now, we will accept the lists of Nova Scotia provided they are not more than a year old, and I believe they are annually prepared. If the machinery here provided under section 32 is allowed to prevail in regard to appeal, I shall be willing to advise my colleagues to accept the Nova Scotia lists, under the condition, of course, that they are not more than a year old. As I say however, I think they are annually prepared in that province. Then we shall have our own franchise and any one who is disfranchised under the law of Nova Scotia could come to the appellate tribunal and be put on the list in accordance with our franchise. If names are improperly on the list they can be stricken off in accordance with section 32; and voters whose names are left off can on election day bring sureties or vouchers with them and cast their votes. That proposal I could accept. I could not however accept the proposal to make these lists absolute and binding, because I do not believe
it is a fair proposal in regard to Ontario. I do not think my hon. friend from West Middlesex and I are,so far apart on the general question but I would insist on the appellate machinery provided in this Bill. New Brunswick, I think, probably offers a Franchise Act more nearly coincident with the present Bill than any of the provinces. I have not read that Act for several weeks and possibly I may be confused as regards its provisions; but my recollection is that it is very nearly the same as this Bill. If their lists are annually prepared they will be accepted; I will accept them unhesitatingly; but I would not allow them to be final. I would allow people to get on those lists in the way provided under section 32.
Now we come to other difficulties. There is Prince Edward Island where they have no voters' list; we must prepare them there. Saskatchewan and Alberta have no voters' lists-I know in Saskatchewan they have not; we .must prepare them there. Other provinces have varying periods for preparing the lists-not annual preparation but longer periods. There the lists may be too old in every instance and we would have to provide the machinery to prepare lists. But, while personally I have had no experience whatever under the Saskatchewan law-I have never taken any part in an election in the province,-I am assured on all hands and by representatives, I think, of all parties, that in. the two elections that have been held under Saskatchewan law, there has been absolutely no complaint- no party has objected. The machinery provided by section 32 is very nearly the Saskatchewan law; it is adapted from the law o'f that province. If it has worked well there, will it not work well here? We do not want to lose control of the machinery. We are willing to accept your lists where you have lists; and where you have not, we give as fair a method as we know how to provide to get those lists.
I say to my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's-who is now in the House-* that as in Nova Scotia they have an annual preparation of provincial voters' lists I accept that part of his proposal, but I cannot say I would accept the proposal to make them absolute and complete. If my hon. friend wants a plain statement in the Act that the provincial lists there shall be accepted, with power to add to them or take from them as provided by section 32, I see no reason why we cannot agree upon that proposal. Similarly in the province of Ontario; and I have had a better oppor-

tuiiity of reading the Bill now before the legislature of that province and a better opportunity of reading the motion and amendment which my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Boss) suggested. I think my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's sees what I am trying to arrive at. It has been pointed out in this House, and has been pointed out to me on other occasions by representatives from Nova Scotia, that under the Nova Scotia lists as framed for provincial purposes two years and even three years may possibly elapse before a man is legally qualified to vote. The dates are so conflicting, or the periods are so tightly drawn, that there is a possibility, they tell me, of a anan being twenty-three years of age before he can vote, even if he had only come of age just before the first day after the first of January in any particular year. As the hon. member for Digby and Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) pointed out, some men may be disqualified for two or three years by some residence qualification; under this. Act they would not. Now there should be an opportunity to add to the lists the names of these men; the provincial lists should not be accepted as final and complete. All that we ask is that machinery provided for that purpose, or for that adding to, shall be the machinery provided in section 32. But, as against some of the other provinces we will have to provide elaborate machinery because there are no up-to-date lists at all.
However, I am glad the discussion has taken place, and it may be continued for that matter. I cannot give the final decision in regard to the suggestions of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's and my hon. friend from West Middlesex; what I have stated on the matter expresses my own views.

I did not hear the whole of the minister's statement, but I think that what I did hear is perhaps the essence of the situation with regard to the Nova Scotia lists, and I am very glad that the minister is disposed to receive even 'n part the suggestions I ventured to offer. With regard to a man being twenty-three or twenty-four years of age before he can vote, I suppose that a man who became twenty-one years of age after the last Dominion election will be twenty-five years before he gets a vote. If you have an annual list I do not see what better you can do; I do not see how you oan devise any better system.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Under the machinery that we create a man who only became
[Hr. Guthrie. 1
twenty-one about two weeks before the election would get on the list providing he lived in the riding.

With regard, however, to the more important question I am very glad to have an assurance of the minister's willingness to accept the Nova Scotia lists for a certain purpose; but when he says that he will not accept them as final, and then goes on to remark that they ought to be added to or substracted from by the machinery he has provided here, does he mean that that will he done by the appointment of registrars?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, because in the urban districts the application goes before the judge of the county, or in case more than one judge is necessary, before an appointee of the county judge. In the country districts it would be before the registrar; but in the country districts the matter is not of so much consequence, because a man who is not on the list can on polling day go and vote .anyway if he swears himself in. It is in the cities that the matter becomes more important because there is no privilege of going on election day and tendering the oath and getting the ballot. The point is this, as my hon. friend will see: The people of Nova Scotia say they have a grievance in the appointment of a sheriff as the revising officer. Sheriffs are not lawyers- I pointed all this out a minute ago-they have no legal qualifications more than the ordinary qualifications of a sheriff in serving a writ or a subpoena, or something of the kind, or the enforcement of the criminal law of the country; they have no education that will train them to decide a question of law in regard to the franchise. But the judges have. I understand from hon. members on this side of the House that time after time motions have been moved in the legislature to allow the judges to be the final court of revision, hut the Provincial Government refuse every time the request is made. They say, "No, we will stick to the sheriff." This Bill proposes that the judges, who are much better qualified to discharge this duty than the sheriff, shall act. Another objection urged upon me is that the sheriff is responsible to the Attorney General. The sheriff is responsible in Ontario. He belongs to the Attorney General's Department, and when the sheriff needs advice he asks the Attorney General for it. They tell me the sheriffs also do so in the province of Nova Scotia.	-
Why not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then if the case comes up for decision, and the sheriff asks for advice the Government that appointed him may and can remove him.
They can only remove him for cause.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
For partisanship and
improper dealing. I do- not say that such actually exists, but the system is quite open to the charge that it may be abused. Now that can be removed if the simple procedure of this Bill is adopted. Why does my hon. friend object to this procedure? Why does he object to these appeals being heard by a judge or by some appointee of the judge? I think the judge would appoint a qualified man if more than one person is necessary for the decision of the question. The element of expense is utterly removed because we are going to adopt the provincial lists of Nova Scotia. The question of appeals will often involve some expense but not much expense; there will be a limited number of appeals in every riding. But that is what is urged upon me by hon. members from Nova Scotia, and it is not only urged upon me but it meets with my approval, therefore my judgment agrees with theirs in the matter. I think it most improper to ask an appointee of the Government, such as the sheriff, to decide these appeals when that sheriff knows that if he does wrong in the eyes of the Government they can cut his head off. They not only appoint him but they have the power to remove him. When he gets into a tangle or into a legal difficulty he asks the Attorney General and the Attorney General is the head of the department that is affected in connection with these voters' lists. That leaves the door pretty wide open for the charge that there may be wrong-doing some day and the possibility of that will be removed if the machinery proposed in section thirty-two for appeals or for additions to the list is adopted.

Of course there are a
thousand and one duties for which the county judge, or any judge, is qualified by his legal training, and for which the sheriff will not be qualified. But I believe it to be the experience in Nova Scotia-I understand it is so, I have not been of late years so intimately associated with the province by residence as formerly-that the decisions of the sheriff as a rule are accepted and very little exception is taken to those decisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What is my hon. friend's objection to what is proposed?

I am coming to that in a moment. While I admit at once that on a. thousand and one questions a judge is the more competent man, I do not think the mere deciding of whether Smith or Brown should go on the voter's list is a great legal question at all-it is a question that any honest and intelligent, layman can determine. That is why I do not think it is so vital that a judge should do it; that is one point. The next point is that my hon. friend says that the Government appoints him, and the. Government can dismiss him. Suppose I were to say that the Government appoints a judge, and the Government can dismiss him?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.

My hon. friend overlooks the vital point, that the judge is appointed for life, and no government can dismiss him according to their displeasure. The same condition applies to the appointment of a sheriff. His appointment is permanent in the sense that he holds office during good behaviour. My hon. friend as a lawyer and administrator knows what that means. A sheriff cannot be dismissed because he has displeased the particular government of the day in connection with the electoral lists.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

No, no. I gave an instance of a sheriff who had been in office 43 years, but my hon. friend says the Government can dismiss him. That is not reasonable, for it is neither in accordance with the law nor with the facts. However, I do not want to press that point too far. There is some force in what my hon. friend says, and if there is any sincere belief on the part of any one that the decisions in Nova Scotia are partisan, and he wants an appeal, I will be perfectly content to have it said that in any such case an appeal shall be made to a county judge; but I do not want it to be made to a reviser, to a registrar or to an enumerator. I do not think it is fair that an enumerator appointed by a returning officer, who may be a partisan, and who is going to be appointed perhaps because he is a partisan, should be allowed to say the final word, I would accept that amendment that the lists of Nova Scotia as revised by the sheriffs shall be subject to appeal to the county judge. I do not want any man left off the lists who is entitled to vote. I want to point out to my hon. friend that while he emphasizes the appeal to the judge, as

a matter of fact the appeal is going to be largely to the registrar, for there are constituencies in Nova Scotia in which there are no cities at all, practically speaking, and it is only in urban centres that the appeals can be referred to the judge. I would accept with pleasure a provision for appeal from the sheriff to the county judge; but I do not think it is fair to take the appeal from the sheriff to an officer who is appointed mainly because he is a partisan.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend understands the Act. He speaks of an enumerator, but an enumerator has no power to make any final binding judgment in the matter. Let me put the case as it will be. We will assume under this clause as drawn that the lists of Nova Scotia are not a year old, in which case they become the voters' lists. Now, I am going to take a rural division. There may be some people who have come into that riding and lived there the requisite time, which is only 60 days, but although entitled to vote they are not on the list. They go to the registrar and ask to be put on. We will assume that he is a crook and does not want to do his duty, and says, "No, I will not put you on." That is not final. It would be a convenience to have the man's name put on. But supposing the officer is crooked and fails in his duty, all that man has to do on election day is to go to the polling station, take the necessary oath, and he becomes entitled to vote. If there was a final binding decision from the enumerator to the registrar I would oppose it; but we have safeguarded it, and I think it is the best safeguard ever embodied in a Franchise Act. In the urban division, as my hon. friend will see, the appeal is to the judge. I cannot make it any clearer. I could not consent to the sheriff being the final revising officer. What I said when my hon. friend was out I may as well say now, that whether well-founded or ill-founded there is a settled feeling on the part of hon. members from Nova Scotia sitting on this side of the House that they do not get fair treatment under the Provincial Franchise Act. I am told by some of those members that they are under a tremendous handicap at every election, and under the circumstances I cannot accept those lists as final. Those hon. members are convinced that they are right and it seems so eminently proper to adopt the course I suggest of leaving the matter to the judge that I do not feel that I need labour the point any longer.

What my hon. friend puts forward as an appeal or remedy does not commend itself to my judgment. Per-nap* it was discussed when I was not here, but the idea that a man shall be allowed to go to the poll and swear himself on at the last moment is to my mind a very objectionable feature of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There has been a qualification of that. I propose, when this section is discussed, to add an amendment providing that two resident ratepayers of the polling subdivision will swear that a man is entitled and qualified to vote, and that he himself will swear the same, the names of the three will be entered in the poll book and he will be entitled to vote. I think that is a safeguard.

The whole idea seems to me to be utterly unsound. However, at the most the hon. gentleman is only interposing an extra cog in the machine. If the sheriff is partisan-and I cannot see any justification for taking that ground because his appointment is made by the local government; however, let us waive that; if there is any suspicion that- the decision of the sheriff is partisan-I would welcome any machinery which would take the case direct to the county judge, I do not care in what form, whether you call it an appeal or anything else. But I am afraid any machinery that will allow enumerators or registrars the right to strike off or put on names without the right of appeal to the county judge is not sound. Why not revise the Bill so that in case a man is dissatisfied at being left off the list he can go direct to the county judge and get a decision?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend objects to a man swearing himseluf on at election day. I am told that under the Nova Scotia Act one man can swear on 500 names.

That has been done
in New Glasgow.

I do not know what
the hon. gentleman means.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That I can go to some
court or tribunal there and on my affidavit I can swear to the qualifications of as long a list of names as I like, and those names will be accepted.

In the making up of
the list.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The only man who can change that is the sheriff. That is a pretty easy way of getting on. That was permitted

under the Franchise Act of 1885 and was condemned as the most unholy thing in it. I think that the method adopted hy this Bill is much better.
My hon. friend ignores the most material fact, that he can swear that list only if he can satisfy the tribunal that it is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: And that tribunal is the sheriff.
He cannot by his own affidavit put men on the list unless he gives good grounds to the revisers, and if the revisers are not satisfied they will not put those men on.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If it is possible for one man to do that, can there be any objection to three men swearing to one vote? That is the proposal of this Bill.

I want tribunals established by law, not some individual to swear men on the list. The tribunals established in Nova Scotia as far as I know are fair and try to be just, although there are exceptions I have no doubt on one side or the other, human nature being what it is. But I come back to the point. I want to avoid trouble, and if a man is not on the list he should have an opportunity of being put-on. My hon. friend can devise any machinery he thinks best to allow a person to go direct from the sheriff to the county judge without the intervention of a partisan registrar.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This Bill permits that.

It does at a - later
stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No. If your provincial list is less than a year old we accept it. Suppose you are not on that list, and suppose you do not go near the registrar, you can go to the county judge. That is provided here. You can go with notice or without notice; you can go without any certificate. That is absolutely provided in the Bill.
The registrar certainly has the power to add and strike off names.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Suppose he will not do it for you?
That is another cog in the machine,-that you can go to the county judge. I see no need of that additional piece of machinery.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to overload the courts, you know.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I intervene to make a suggestion? The Ontario Government is introducing a Bill which will affect this proposed legislation so far as the preparation of lists is concerned. That circumstance has altered very materially the significance of this section. What the minister said this evening about the willingness of himself and his colleagues to accept as a basis the provincial lists also goes^ a very considerable way toward removing some of the very serious doubts so many of us entertained about the purpose of the Government in the section as drafted. Now, we have before the Committee different suggestions, one from the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), which the minister is prepared to accept in part and to consider further; one from the member for Middlesex West (Mr. Ross) which also the minister has expressed his approval of in part and his willingness to consider further. I suggest that before we pass this clause the minister might be agreeable to having a short conference with the member for Shelburne and Queen's, the member for Middlesex West, the member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), with a view to seeing just how far-
Don't do it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I hear my
hon. friend say: "Don't do it." I ask him if that is the spirit in which we ought to try to work out a Franchise Act?
You would not be satisfied anyway.
What do you know about it?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We should all approach a matter of such great consequence as this in the spirit of trying to get an Act which will appeal to the people as being fair and just. A conference might help to remove a great deal of doubt and establish a wider ground of certitude; more could be accomplished in that way than by hours of debate here. What we have heard to-day suggests the possibility of our getting very much closer together on this particular section than I thought was possible when the discussion started. Let me illustrate just what I have to say, because I have Ontario more particularly in mind. When this Bill was introduced we had before us only the Ontario lists as prepared under the late Hearst Government. They were prepared on the system of enumeration, and as this section read at that time



it meant that if a general election took place within a year, the lists which we would have to use so far as Ontario was concerned would be the lists that the Hearst Government had prepared for the last election. If it did not take place within a year, or at any time up to November of this year, then we would have no alternative than that of the appointment by the Government of its army of enumerators to prepare the lists in accordance with the machinery provided by this Act. That, we all felt, would be dangerous and anything but satisfactory. Now, what has happened since this Bill was introduced. The Drury Government have come into office; they have thrown the old Hearst legislation to the winds, and are drafting a new law and providing for the preparation of annual lists. The minister tells us to-night that if that law is in force, then these annual lists will be used by the federal Government for the purposes of elections. That is an entirely different situation from that with which we were confronted when the Bill was first brought into the House; and, as I say, for that reason we are very much closer together than I saw any possibility of our being in the early stages of the discussion. In view of the attitude of the minister toward the suggestions that have been made from this side I feel that if he is agreeable to a conference of this kind, simply to smooth out the differences as between the different provinces, we should probably be much closer together at the end of an hour's conference of that kind than we would be at the conclusion of a prolonged discussion here.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No matter which way
we decide that point, the clause has to go, because if no lists are made within twelve * months by the province, we shall have to prepare new ones. In some provinces they have no lists any way, so we have to go on and consider the clause. But as it affects particularly, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Ontario I quite agree with my hon. friend; we would let that aspect of it stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
That is the
aspect of it that 1 would like to have stand. In order to make clear the effect of the law as it would be if we passed this section, let me put a question to the minister. Assuming that an election were to take place in Canada within a year of the time the Drury Government was formed, that is, before November of this year, then that election would be held on the lists used in the last provincial election?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If they were not more than twelve months old.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If an election came before November of this year, the lists used for federal purposes so far as Ontario is concerned would be the lists that were used in the last provincial election. Now if the general election came in December, before the law now being drafted in Ontario was put into motion, then the lists would be prepared by enumerators in accordance with the provisions of this Act. without any reference whatever to the law that the Ontario Government is putting through at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, unless lists were
prepared under that law.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Assuming that the Ontario law were now passed and that lists were prepared under it by November or December of this year then those lists would be used?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They would be valid for twelve months.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
But if they
were not prepared until say March or April of next year and a general election took place before then, lists would be prepared under the provisions of this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, I understand that the proposal is that the Ontario Bill shall be passed and that the provincial lists for this year shall be prepared under it. I understand that they have to be prepared for municipal purposes in any case.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I simply wanted to make the point clear.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that the Ontario law will be in force by December next, anyway. There might be a month or two after November and before the new provincial lists come during which, if a general election were held, we might have to prepare new lists.
Do I understand that there is no appeal from the lists as prepared by Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Oh yes, there is.

Because I would very
much object to that. Hon. members know that in the old days it used to cost us anything from $100 to $1,000 a year to look after our lists. Why should members of the federal House have to provide the machinery for the revision of lists for Ontario? When hon. gentlemen opposite were in office and had charge virtually of all the clerks and

all the printing shops, when we had our lists revised and fixed up they would go to the printer, and then, when they were there they would be hocus-pocussed and a lot of old Conservatives would find themselves without votes. I would not agree to any such proposal as that there should be a constant revision of lists by members of this House. There must be revision before a general election; that is sufficient. Now hon. gentlemen opposite are asking for a conference. Of course, it is all right enough to ask for a conference; it is all right to compromise.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am not asking; I am making a suggestion.

I have the floor for the moment, if you please. Hon. gentlemen opposite would have a conference and then they would go before the country and say that they forced the minister to give them this fine election law. For it is a fine law. I do not agree with any hon. member who wants to have a special law for his own province. The law should be the same for all provinces. There should be no difference; no distinction. An appeal should be provided for a man at the last moment who has been, by some means, deprived of his vote. I am not going to put confidence in the Government of Ontario. The gentleman who leads it has been looking after voters' lists in my riding, and I know how difficult it is to keep track of him; he is a past master in the art of dropping names from the voters' lists. It may work out to the advantage of the public that there shall be an annual list for which the municipalities pay. The fact of the matter is that the Government at Toronto is unloading the expense of preparing its lists. I cannot see that there is anything to be gained by going into any conference, if [DOT] this Bill is satisfactory and if hon. gentlemen opposite can bring forward no valid reasons or grounds for complaint. I have listened for hours to hon. gentlemen opposite discussing the matter, and I do not see any valid objection that can be raised. In particular, I see no objection to the way in which the list is handled in Nova Scotia, and I cannot see any reason why the list there should be handled differently from the way in which lists are handled in the other provinces. Moreover, I cannot see why my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) is so anxious that the sheriff should have all the say in regard to this matter; there is something wrong, there is something suspicious 150*
in all that clamour to have the sheriff do this work. For that reason I would object to that, and if I were the minister, I would not concede that point. If hon. gentlemen opposite are determined to fight the matter out, let them do so; but as regards holding a conference, the conference might not last five minutes; my hon. friends might say: Change one or two words here and there and then the clause will be all right; and then they would go broadcast over the country and say that they forced the Government to give them this law. The Government is responsible, and if there is anything wrong in this measure, I would say: Let the onus rest upon the Government and let the Opposition assume no responsibility for it.

It is refreshing to listen to my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) and to size him up by his own opinion of others and how he views questions of this kind in the House. He is responsible for his actions, so let him take the responsibility for it.
We have responsible Government.

What I rose to ask is this: The Acting Solicitor General has spoken about every province except Quebec. I asked him why the one-year limitation was inserted, and he replied that the lists might get stale, and there is something in that contention. But this is the position. I understand the first object of the law is to facilitate the franchise to people. In Quebec, we have this condition, that the lists in the large cities are revised only every even-numbered year. Every year in rural municipalities and in towns and villages the lists are made by municipal councils, and the question of plugging could not come up with us, because the lists are made from the assessment roll, and the assessor has to indicate on the assessment roll who is a resident and who is a non-resident. A man who is a non-resident under the Quebec Election Act has no right to vote.
When did that change take place?
I think the change was made two years ago.	[DOT]
Four years.
In every other province dual voting has been abolished for the last twenty years.
What is the difference?
This shows how Ear you are ahead of u-s.

Do not think you are virtuous Ontario as against Quebec when you come before the House and accuse one another of plugging and stealing elections and stealing ballot boxes and having to pay money. Why, my hon. friend is a self-confessed man who has to spend money to make his lists.
I do.
Why?
My hon. friend is a lawyer and can look after his lists. I have to hire an attorney to look after mine.

I do not have to hire an attorney or anything else. The list is passed and the man who finds his name is not on the list goes to the revising officer and asks that his name be put on. In rural municipalities the council sits as a court of revision, if you like, and people appear before that court. I am not put to any expense in the matter except as regards postage for writing to some fellows telling them to look up the lists and see if their names are on. But be that as it may, if you want to facilitate the franchise, you must have something to start on in large cities because, if you have no names on the lists to start with, and you post up notices and tell the people to register, names are going to be left off.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In London, England, in New York and similar places, that is the way in which the lists are made up, namely by personal registration.

That may be. If you
accept the last list in the .rural municipalities, why not accept the last list used in a provincial election in the larger cities?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How old might the list be?

It would not be over
two years old. In Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, Sherbrooke, St. Hyacinthe and Hull, the lists are revised in March or April of every even-numbered year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Then you would have
to see to it that an election took place every odd-numbered year, and in that case 1923 wmuld be all right because then the list would be only one year old.

The matter all depends
on the month. If you had an election in July, my list -would be no good.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Make it September.

If you have it in February, 1922, I would be in the same position, because the revision is in the even-numbered years. Last year the lists were revised in March or April, I forget which. If you have an election in June, 1921, my list is no good and you have to start with absolutely nothing. It is only fair to make an exception in these cases that the last lists in large cities which have a revision every even-numbered year 'shall 'be the list to be used. Then you will have something to start on and names can be added or struck off. I am not objecting to the appeals at all, but I want something to start on; and if you do not accept these lists, you would start without a single name and you would have to bring the people to the registrar and have them register. That is a new departure; we have had no election under that system except the one in Quebec East; and a great many people would lose their votes. I would not ask the minister to accept lists two years old when lists one year old or less than that can be had, but we could make the exception in the case of large cities by adding after the words: " for the purposes of provincial elections" the words "except in such cities where revision of lists is biennial." That would cover Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers, Sherbrooke, St. Hyacinthe and Hull.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Are those the only
places?
Yes, in our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member's suggestion is that in those places the last list should be the one to be used with power to add to and strike off as in this clause.

In Ontario, in a number of cities and towns, as a matter of fact, 'the list is nearly a year old. The list is prepared from the assessment roll, and the list that is prepared from the assessment roll in Toronto is a year old before	it appears before
the public. The same thing is true of one of the towns in my riding, and I think the same is true of Guelph, but these lists just form the basis and they are pretty nearly within the year. 'If we are going to have exceptions made for everywhere we shall never get anywhere. We must have a general law applicable all over the Dominion. As a matter of fact, if I were appointed an enumerator in Montreal I would certainly start with the old list.
It is easier to start with the old list than to get voters to register.
You would know the voters who lived in the wards.
I do not think this is an exception. It is kind of general. Here is a class of cities-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It may be a broad exception, but it is an exception.

In discussing the question of accepting provincial lists the minister referred to Prince Edward Island and said we had to make a list for that province as there was no list there. I cannot see why the minister comes to that conclusion. I was rather amused at the controversy between the hon. members (Mr. Currie) and (Mr. Bureau), each claiming that his province' was ahead of the other. I think the province of Prince Edward Island is further advanced than any other province, because we did away with lists entirely over twenty years ago. We have, of couree, qualifications for voters. I can see no reason why there should not be uniform qualifications all over Canada, but I would ask the minister to follow at Dominion elections the method of voting in force in the different provinces. In Prince Edward Island the voters know their qualifications. They are posted up in the proclamation, and the voters go to the poll and vote. It is true that we have very few of an alien population. About 95 per cent of our electors are residents of many years standing and they are well known. To make a list for Prince Edward Island would simply be doubling or trebling the cost of holding the election there. There are only four constituencies, and I cannot see any purpose in going to an expenditure of $20,000 or $25,000 in making a list that is absolutely of no use so far as the pronvince of Prince Edward Island is concerned. If the minister would look at the (qualifications required for the local legislature, and the method of holding provincial elections in the province, I think he would see that nothing could be gained by making a list for our province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Are there no property qualifications in your franchise?

I hope the minister has caught my point, which is that the qualifications of voters should be the same all over the Dominion, but that the method of holding the election should be that followed in each of the provinces, so the oualification of voters does not apply to
the point I am making. The qualifications are as follows:
Every person shall be entitled to vote at an election to be held for the election of an Assemblyman to represent in the Legislative Assembly of this province, any Electoral District: If such person
(a)	Is of the full age of twenty-one years on the day of the election, and is not by this Act or any law of the'province disqualified or prevented from voting; and
(b)	Is a male British subject; and-
Then follow further qualifications, for instance, if the man has paid his poll tax for the year preceding he is entitled to vote, or if he is the owner of a freehold estate.
How much is the poll tax?
Two dollars. He must have his receipt for that poll tax. If he has that, and is a British subject twenty-one years of age, he is entitled to vote.
Are there any property qualifications?

That does not matter if he has paid his poll tax. If lie' is above the age when the poll tax is payable, there are other qualifications. In Prince Edward Island, for instance, where the people are not mixed with aliens, and where everybody is well known, I see no reason why the minister should not follow the method of holding the poll that is to be adopted in the provincial elections. I think the expense of making these lists is not justified so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned. You could have the same qualifications of voters all over Canada, but the method of holding the election should he one used in the different provinces at provincial elections.
Is there any residence qualification?
They must reside in the province twelve months and in the district one month.
There is no list made of those who are entitled to vote?
None whatever.
What protection is there against people from other districts coming in to vote?

The candidate's
agents are at the polls and it is their duty to see that nobody votes who is not entitled to vote in that division.
[DOT]2360

There are no lists in a
city of 20,000?
We have no cities of that size.

Has not Charlottetown
a population of about 15,000?
Mr. J. E, SINCLAIR: Only 12,000.
And there is no trouble?

None whatever.
There was more trouble with the lists in 1917, the people not being acquainted with registering themselves, than we had in all previous elections over a number of years.
What is the time allowed previous to an election for paying the poll tax?

It must be paid the year previous to the election. The poll tax for the year is not due until December, so if an election was held in September they would have to show the receipt for the year previous.

There is what I might
call a double franchise in Prince Edward Island. One half the members of the legislature are called councillors, and the other half are called assemblymen:	That arog*
in this way: We had a legislative council there at one time, and it was a very difficult thing to abolish, because the councillors naturally were reluctant to abolish themselves. The Prime Minister, however of that day, introduced a Bill, and we must assume that he talked nicely to these gentlemen of the legislative council, twelve in number, and told them: You will be councillors still after you have abolished your chamber; you will be elected to the assembly. In that way he managed to persuade these councillors to abolish themselves, and from that day to this we have the peculiar condition of having councillor electors and assemblymen electors. The councillor electors require a property qualification amounting to $325, and those who vote for the assemblymen must have paid their poll tax; it is practically manhood suffrage in their case. When, these two classes of members elected to the legislature come into the chamber and take their seat, no one can tell which of them is councillor and which an assemblyman. There are fifteen electoral districts in the province, and each district sends one councillor and one assemblyman to the legislature. A not very strong party man might be disposed to attempt to cross his votes, but he cannot do it very successor. J. E. Sinclair.]
fully in this case. He has to vote for councillor and for an assemblyman if he polls two votes. He is not allowed to vote for two councillors or two assemblymen, but for one of each. That is the peculiar condition we have in the province so far as elections to the legislature are concerned.
As to the manner of holding the elections and the preparations therefor, there are no lists. The districts are mostly rural and everybody is supposed to know everybody else. Charlottetown has a population of 12,000 and there are incorporated towns and villages, but generally speaking the people know one another pretty well, and the candidate's agents are supposed to know who are entitled to vote. For my part I think it is rather a chaotic and precarious way of carrying on an election and I am in favour of having lists of some description. Every one who is qualified to vote for an assemblyman-that is to say, every one who is twenty-one years of age and has the other necessary qualifications as to residence, poll tax, etc.,-is qualified to vote for members of the House of Commons. As regards women voters, I may say that, so far, women have not been allowed to vote for members of the provincial legislature. In the Dominion elections in 1917, of course, it is well known, certain women were given the vote. Under this Act they will be given the franchise, and that fact of itself, in my opinion, should be a cogent reason why we should have voters' lists. I should not like to see elections carried on in that province, especially for members of the House of Commons, in the rather antiquated way in which they have been conducted for the legislature, without lists. I do not think it is a proper way, and for my part I am quite satisfied to have this clause go through as it is. The Bill generally, I think will meet conditions in Prince Edward Island, so far as I am able to judge; and I think I am safe in saying that- it will be generally acceptable to the people of that province. I do not think it would be well to continue, in the election of members for the House of Commons, the practice in vogue in Prince Edward Island in connection with the election of assemblymen, for I think it is very much behind the times.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Do I understand that
you retain the names of non-residents on your list?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is objectionable. Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR:	The reviser is
instructed to put every man and woman on the reviser's list, if he finds that they are qualified by the assessment roll to the extent of $160 real estate and $300 personal estate. In the case of fishermen it is $150, which represents boats, nets, etc. So that every class of person in the province who has anything in the way of property is covered. There is a provision that absence up to .four months in the case of an income voter does not interfere with his qualification. Under our law a student who is in college is regarded as living at home, and provision is made for sailors. When you come to deal with all these cases, therefore, the question of residence does not amount to much.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have been informed
that under the system whereby voters' lists in Nova 'Scotia are prepared, a resident in that province can go to the reviser and by his own affidavit swear on the names of, say, 100 men, and the reviser has no option. He must accept that oath and put those names on. There is an appeal against that to the sheriff, but the difficulty is to find the men. Where they have to be notified and have personally to appear you cannot prosecute an appeal because you 11 p.m. cannot find these men to give them notice. That has been represented to me as one great objection to the system in Nova Scotia and I should like some information.
Mr. J .H. SINCLAIR:	Does the minister say that the men must come personally and apply for themselves in every case? If so, it is going to be very difficult to comply with the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I asked the question
about your law; I do not know anything about it.

It is true that one person who knows the facts can apply for another person in the province of Nova Scotia. But when my hon. friend talks about one hundred persons, I must say that I do not know of any such case as that. I might know the qualifications of my brother, say, or any man who works for me, and if he were not able to apply personally I could apply for him. That is reasonable, and there may be cases where one man would be better qualified than any one else to make application for a number of men. Take such a man as the cashier of a coal company, or some man who keeps the books of a company and who knows the incomes of the men and their qualifications, the qualifications for income voters, I may remark, is $260. I see no reason why a man who is, let us say, a paymaster and knows all the facts, should not be allowed to make an affidavit. There may be such cases where one man would apply for a number of other men, but it is only in an exceptional case that a man will not be able to go himself and make application.

I would ask the hon. member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr Sinclair) if he thinks that any one man would have sufficient knowledge of five hundred individuals to be able to swear to their qualifications? Yet under such affidavit five hundred names would be added to the list, as was done in the towns of New Glasgow and Trenton.
An -hon. MEMBER: Five hundred?
Yes between the two towns.

What is the difference between a man swearing for one ot for fifty or a hundred, if he has the knowledge? It is admitted all around that it is convenient that one man who has a knowledge of the qualifications of another should make an application for him. We know very well that lots of people are very indifferent as to whether their names are on the list at all, so the poor politician has to look out for himself and see that the names of those perons are put on the list. Our law in Nova Scotia at one time was that each individual had to make application for himself. It was found, however, that the law was not lived up to, that people would not comply with it and it had to be changed. Under the change made one person can

make affidavit as to the qualifications of another. But that is not the last word in the matter. All that enables one to do is to give the names to a reviser.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: And he is bound to accept them.

In the province of Nova Scotia the reviser is not bound to accept the affidavit at all unless it is handed in to him before the twentieth day of January. Very well supposing the names are put in before the twentieth day of January-which very seldom happens because people are not so much on the alert as they should be-the reviser is bound to put those names on his preliminary list. That preliminary list goes through a great many evolutions before it reaches the sheriff. It has to go before a court of three revisers who sit on a certain day and hear evidence as to whether the parties are qualified or not. If I object to anybody who is on the list I can notify him. I am not bound to notify the fellow who made the application for him. I can either notify the man who made the application for him or the man himself by sending him a letter, posted prepaid, to his last known address. Then I can go to the revisers' court and say, "There is a man on the list who should not be on and if I can show by evidence that that man is not qualified his name goes off.
