Now that list which is prepared by the revisers' ,court must be signed by the three revisers. The three of them sign it and put a certi-ficatae on it that such is their decision as to that list. One-half of those who were on the preliminary list may have been struck off, but if there is anybody dissatisfied with the decision of that board he has the right to appeal to the sheriff. The three revisers are seldom of one political complexion. I do not remember ever seeing a board with three Liberals or three Tories except for the fourteen years I was in our town council when we had a Tory board. But there was never any trouble; they were honest men and they did the right thing. It is a mistake to think that because a man hands in a name bo one of the revisers that is the end of it; there are three or four sittings before the list is signed by the three revisers. All three, honest and capable men sitting in that way must be satisfied that the list is all right before they sign it.

What would you do in a case where you could not find the man who made the affidavit, where in fact there was no such man in existence? In the case I have referred to the name was John Smith and there was no John Smith.
I would not care a button about the man who made the application if I could find the man whose name was on the list-that is all that is necessary for me.
Suppose you could not find him either??

I could make application to the board and prove that the man's address is unknown->1 put my evidence before the board, and if they are honest and capable men they will strike the name off. I can say, "There is no such man in existence, this thing is a bogus application, this man should go off the list.," and surely if I could satisfy a board of three capable, honest men-such as I have no doubt you would find on the board in New Glasgow- that would be all that would be necessary. I cannot conceive of having a revising board, for example in the town of New Glasgow, that would not do the square thing about the voters' list. I appeal to my hon. friend (Mr. McGregor) who comes from New Glasgow as to whether that is not the case? I do not know of any town in Nova Scotia, Pictou or anywhere else, where we could get three honest men who would solemnly take their oath and sit down and revise the list, who would do anything that was crooked in the performance of their duty. I put it up to my hon. friend (Mr. Mcgregor) whether he thinks for one moment that Sheriff Harris of the town of Pictou would be party to anything crooked about the list. Now I put it up to him to say whether Sheriff Harris is not square in his dealings?

I want to say to the hon. member that the revisers of the town have no option in the matter whatever: they have to take the affidavit. Nobody knows that better than the hon. member who has just taken his seat. As to the sheriff he can only deal with these cases when the men are brought before him. You cannot bring the men before him because in many cases they do not exist. But they turn up at election day, and that is the reason their names are added. _

The hon. member need not put supposititious cases to me. As to putting on the list the name of a man who was sworn to as having the qualifications and being qualified in every respect, and then not being able to find him, I never heard of such a case. If there is such a case in New Glasgow it stands solitary and alone as far as I have heard.

For the benefit of the hon. member, let me tell him that the system

referred to is a very old form of (political corruption that used to have much vogue in the province of Ontario. In so stating I am sorry the member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) is not here-with apologies to him, I may say. What has been complained of is what is known as the colonizing of voters. We have done away with the property qualification. When we had the property qualification in the case of a man who owned a large number of town lots, the system was to put names down as being the owners. Those names would be handed in and would be put on the voters' list the same as they are in Nova Scotia, but that difficulty does not exist and such names will be struck off the list. In the old days a lot of names could be put on the list but you could never find the men although they always turned up on election day. There were a lot of those chaps and they wrould vote according to the way the man who paid them wished. That is an old form of corruption. Where you have dual voting and property qualifications you are almost sure to have colonization of voters.
An Ontario virtue.
Take the city of Montreal. A friend of the hon. gentleman told me the other day that in the good old days he could give as many votes as he wanted in this way for members of Parliament.
He was boasting.

He did not have to do
much boasting to do that. He could just ride around and if there was property in each riding he could vote in respect of it. That is what we call colonizing. The names of foreigners used to be used for the purpose, and when the foreigners were brought in why, "All coons look alike",-you could not tell whether they were qualified or not.
Well, the coons are going to get the vote this time.

Now, in Ontario we have one man one vote, and the individual must be pretty well identified before he can vote for a member of the House of Commons. There is no. merit whatever in the claim of the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) because what he has reference to is an old form that used to be followed in the preparation of the list many years ago, and it was characterized by the most rampant form of corruption that this country had ever seen. What we call the colonizing of voters is not possible under this Bill. That
the hon. member should make any such proposition is to my mind very surprising. It shows that he is not familiar with what has been done in various parts of the country if he insists on having such a provision in this legislation.

I do not understand what the hon. member means, when he suggests that I have any knowledge of any such corrupt system. I never heard of it in the province of Nova Scotia, it does not exist. If there are such things carried on in the province of Ontario I am very sorry for the old, well-settled and reputable province if that is the fruit of their Christianity and civilization. We have no records of such corruption in Nova Scotia. I was simply pointing out the way by which honest men get their names on the list. If my hon friend doubts my word, I challenge him or any other hon. member to produce any statement of mine in this House that was not well founded on fact, for I am too sensitive of my honour to make any statement except what is absolutely true.

I do not dispute the statement of the hon. member that he is justified in his remarks; but to have a gentleman of his standing propose The insertion of a clause in this Bill that would permit the commonest form of corruption that is known all over the United States and England as "colonizing voters" is to me very surprising. That system has been abolished in every decent community. Why, twenty years ago that is how Tammany Hall used to carry New York.

Is that where you got
your schooling?

I know of no corruption. In the town immediately adjoining where I live, Sydney Mines, there are 5,000 or 6,000 men employed, and every dollar of wages paid to those men passes through the hands of a paymaster. He has the list of their earnings and knows what their income is. Those men go down into the mines at seven o'clock in the morning and do not come up until late in the afternoon and probably they would not have time to go before the registrar and make personal application to be put on the list. Supposing they said to their paymaster: You know our qualifications, and the law allows you to make this application for us. Go and make the application. I can see no corruption in that being done; it is only a mere matter of convenience which the statute has allowed for very many years. In Nova Scotia we

have a very vigorous and capable opposition, but I never heard any of its members demand that that law should be repealed.

I would suggest an
amendment to the clause by inserting after the word "elections" in the twenty-fifth line the words "in the case of cities where the revision is biennial the last revised list shall be the voters' list." The object, as I was stating just now, is to facilitate voting. In Montreal, Quebec, Sherbrooke, St. Hyacinthe and Hull the revision is only by-annually. Therefore if an election takes place, say, in the month of July, we would have no lists whatever under the Act. This would make it just the same as our provincial law. Unless something like this is incorporated in the Bill I think we shall have confusion in our province, because large numbers of people seeing their names on the list made from the assessment rolls would not think of going near the registrar to be registered. This list, although more than one year old, could be utilized in such a case.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As we will have to pass the clause anyway to apply to all the other provinces, and as there is no objection to the wording' of the clause in general, I would suggest that we pass it and to-morrow confer on the proposals that have been made to see if we can arrange anything satisfactory with regard to the suggestions from Ontario, Quebec, and Nova Scotia.

Under the Act as it
stands and as the minister understands it now, how long before election day will the lists be completed as far as they can be completed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Candidates should have the unrevised list not later than nomination day. The next five days are taken up with revision. It is provided that the candidates shall get the revised list with the final corrections on the ninth day before polling day.

What is the reason for granting an appeal to a man who lives in an incorporated town and not to a man who lives in a country district? For instance, a man who lives in North Sydney has the right of appeal to the county court judge if he is dissatisfied with the work of the registrar; but the man who is immediately beyond the town limits has no appeal at all from the action of the' registrar in the county. I cannot understand why a man who is in the municipal district if he lives beyond the city or town should not

have the same right of appeal as the other man.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is a reason founded very largely in convenience. In Saskatchewan, where the system has been tried and found very satisfactory and where the ridings are very large, it is impossible within any reasonable time to provide machinery to permit the hearing of appeals between the time the lists are made and the election. That is the foundation of the difference between the procedure for the rural and the urban polls. If we had more judges, more judicial officers, and disregarded expense, perhaps we could apply the appellate system in all districts. But the argument was taken up in the Saskatchewan legislature-I get my information on this point from the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder)-and it was well discussed there. But the actual experience is what we base our judgment on; it has worked out to the satisfaction of everybody. Then, in the country districts throughout Ontario I am satisfied that as a rule each elector knows every other elector in the rural division-not absolutely, but as a rule. There are not nearly so many appeals in the country; there are not such difficult points to decide. A man who has been excluded can completely assert his right on polling day. But the making of a distinction was found an inconvenience and an expense, as I understand my colleague the Minister of Immigration.

Why not leave it optional with the man to appeal if he wants to? If persons in rural districts which are close to cities and towns want to have that right, why should it not be given them? Of course, a man living twentydive or thirty miles away might not wish to do this, and the only thing to do is swear him. But if a man chooses to appeal, that is his own look-out. 'If it is difficult; if it is expensive, he need not do it, but if he is willing to go to the trouble of appearing before a judge, why not give him the privilege of doing so?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I see a great number of difficulties in imposing territorial limitations. I see the difliculty of complexity. We have tried to have one system for the rural and. one for the urban division, and to make for greater certainty we are going to put in an amendment that the Chief Electoral Officer shall at the outset decide what is an urban division and what is a rural division and what parts thereof are

such. Then, there is a simple system for the one and a simple system for the other. If you make a dual system for the rural division I do not see where you are going to get any finality. The judge who hears the rural appeals would have to prepare a special list of those appeals. The urban lists are printed at printing offices but the rural lists are not printed, so that the matter might not be concluded before election day. It might be a convenience to people living near a judge to have the advantage of the dual system, but on the whole I think that it cannot work any inconvenience or any injustice to have the provision as it is set forth in the present section.

Perhaps the point has
already been discussed, but I make the suggestion in consequence of what my hon. friend has said; what directions are to be given to the Chief Electoral Officer by which he is to be guided in determining what is urban and what is not?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Just the interpretation
of the section of the Act. Then, under another section he is the absolute judge. I assume that he will communicate with the Provincial Governments and have the latest returns; he will find out from the Governments what are the incorporated towns, cities and villages in the various provinces. Hie will also have if he wishes to avail himself of them, the latest census returns-because we have annual returns in Ontario made up from the assessment rolls. He is at liberty to form his judgment on any data, he sees fit. T have no doubt that his first duty will be to gather together that information and decide, and his discretion is absolute. A place which has a thousand people and is incorporated as a city, town or village is an urban division. But these conditions must both exist-the numbei of people and the incorporation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
No. If it is carried, and we want to introduce amendments, we shall have to go back to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not insist upon it, if it is a bona fide effort we are making.
This clause embraces ten pages of printing.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not mean the
schedules. We must understand this. I do not propose to consider the amendment of the clause as a general principle for the
Dominion of Canada; what we are discussing is the amendment in so far as it pertains to Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. As I have suggested, we must have the clause, no matter what we specially provide for these four places, because there are five other provinces in respect of which the clause must operate.
My grievance is the biennial revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My suggestion was that the clause without the schedules be allowed to carry.
My (amendment would come in the body of the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not necessarily.
Oh, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You could put it in the schedule; you can amend the schedule just as much as the clause. However, I am not going to insist on the point. I wanted to make some progress, that is all.
We have made a lot of progress. That clause will go through in five minutes next time.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well,' we have your undertaking to that effect; why not do it now?
I am not an undertaker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is impossible to carry the clause without carrying it all, and the clause includes the schedules.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understood not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The clause does not include the schedule unless the schedule contains an agreement ratified by the clause. If the clause is carried, the next item of business before the committee will be the consideration of the schedules to clause 32.
If we desire to propose amendments to the clause after it has been .adopted we shall have to obtain unanimous consent to open it up again.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) is quite right in that. If any change is to be made in the clause the clause will have to be reconsidered.
My amendment comes in the clause. There is no place to work it into the schedule. Let it stand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is for the committee to decide. Is the committee ready for the question?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Two amendments are suggested. It may be that at a conference we can reach an understanding. If we can reach an understanding to-morrow, as to-night seems to be probable, we will not bring in these amendments. But if we cannot, we want to bring in the amendments and vote on them.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: My fear is that our labour is all going to be in vain. It happens that on Friday we cannot take up consideration of this Bill. Monday will be well taken up, I understand, with a special order, and on Tuesday there is the Budget. I assume that the Budget will continue until it is finished; so I am sure we shall have forgotten most of the Franchise Act in the interval.
Oh, no; we shall have our amendments written down and agreed upon and it will be all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On that understanding I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 11.35 p.m.
Friday, May 14, 1920.
